almohad_caliphate:
[Surviving territory and communications] The Almohads retain Marrakech, Beni-Mellal Castle, and Debdou Castle. Fez, Salé, and Tangier belong to the Marinids, while the Tunisian centers belong to the Hafsids. The old trans-Maghreb empire is therefore not a present tax district. The caliphate has contracted severely around Marrakech. Atlas valleys offer defensible approaches and potential tribal support, but dispersed positions depend on passes, pack animals, and local cooperation. Cultivated land, irrigation, pasture, and markets near the capital matter more immediately than distant imperial claims. Access toward trans-Saharan routes has value without granting control over every caravan or its profits. Merchants can redirect traffic when protection deteriorates or successive authorities demand incompatible payments.

[Caliphal authority and its changing basis] The dynasty arose from Ibn Tumart's religious movement and the conquests of Abd al-Mu'min. Marrakech embodies that inheritance as well as housing the court. Umar al-Murtada has ruled since 1248. Caliphal dignity and family descent remain political resources, but local leaders no longer necessarily deliver taxes and soldiers simply on command. The strict religious discipline associated with the early movement now coexists with dispersed local power and varied military partnerships. Almohad history includes changing legal emphases, practical diplomacy, and varied military partnerships. For subjects, legitimate government must still provide security for cultivation, exchange, and worship. An appeal to ancestral victories cannot by itself replace those obligations or compel competing elites to agree.

[Revenue and diminishing confidence] Agricultural dues, urban transactions, and passage revenues provide identifiable resources. Rights to collect, the sums gathered locally, and the resources actually reaching the court can differ substantially. With former provinces lost, court expenditure, fortifications, and hired troops must draw on a smaller base, while collection depends on local power. Farmers need seed and food as well as the grain demanded by officials. Merchants judge the entire journey: a modest charge combined with repeated robbery can cost more than a higher payment backed by reliable protection. Recurrent emergency exactions can consequently reduce effective income. Religious property and urban institutions have their own claims; judges, scholars, and local notables matter in settling boundaries, protection, and exemptions.

[Military inheritance and defensive capacity] Tribal organization long structured Almohad recruitment, making chiefs political partners as well as commanders. Arab auxiliary horsemen and soldiers from other backgrounds also served, and later rulers employed Christian mercenaries. The army is not a body with one language, one religious affiliation, and one interest. The loss of provinces and allies concentrates costs on fewer defenders, and delayed wages can send experienced soldiers to another patron. A reduced government needs guarded gates, stores, and passes, and must avoid pursuing an enemy so far that its return is cut off. Cavalry requires fodder and replacement mounts; mercenaries require credible remuneration; agricultural levies remove labor from fields. Walls may delay an assault, but repeated damage to nearby villages undermines the food supply and the defenders' willingness to continue.

[Neighbors and room for negotiation] The Marinids are an established northern competitor with important urban centers, not a momentary disturbance. The Zayyanids farther east and the Hafsids beyond them likewise pursue their own survival and authority. Former caliphal titles no longer constitute enforceable commands. Across the straits, the loss of major Muslim cities during the first half of the century has left Granada pursuing separate accommodations; Andalusian aid cannot be assumed. Trade agreements, presents, limited truces, and ransoming people offer usable alternatives to simultaneous war. Al-Murtada's correspondence with Christian powers leaves avenues for contact alongside religious rivalry. Embassies, credible guarantees, and acceptable obligations are needed to turn any proposed terms into a working agreement.

[Internal costs and open alternatives] Rivalry within the ruling house, resistance to levies among tribal leaders, and urban demands for safety can reinforce one another without creating a single organized opposition. Religious scholars likewise need not support one candidate. A court demanding the resources of its former empire may turn protection into predation; a court making concessions must face accusations that it has diminished inherited dignity. A defensible alternative is to protect the core city, shelter displaced households, preserve limited income, and contract exposed positions when relief is impossible. A supportable capital remains a base for issuing commands, preserving records, and seeking renewed allegiance. Dignity and practical accommodation need not be opposites: protecting dependents may sustain royal standing better than demanding repetition of old oaths without providing the means to honor them.
aragon:
[Land, sea, and royal possessions] The Crown of Aragon links the Ebro interior to the Catalan coast. Its directly available positions include Zaragoza, Barcelona, Valencia, and castles including Castellvell, Begur, and Chinchilla. Agriculture and livestock around Zaragoza, maritime exchange through Catalan ports, and Valencian irrigation make different contributions; the whole realm is not one merchant city. Roads and coastal carriage move supplies but remain subject to seasons, tolls, and hostile positions. The Pyrenees are a barrier, not an impassable wall. Majorca and other conquered territories add maritime connections and obligations, while port income and ship availability still depend on specific privileges and payments. Irrigation channels, cultivated plots, and surviving communities in Valencia determine whether conquest can support lasting royal revenue.

[The law of a composite crown] James I has ruled since 1213 and draws prestige from conquests including Majorca and Valencia. His authority nevertheless operates through distinct legal traditions, noble rights, and urban privileges. Which law applies in a conquered district affects jurisdiction, officeholding, and rents. The Aragonese legal compilation of 1247 is relevant; nobles draw on legal tradition to defend their standing against arbitrary interference. The Treaty of Corbeil with Louis IX in 1258 settles old French claims over Catalonia and James's claims in southern France. It provides a framework for northern accommodation, reducing northern commitments and allowing consolidation while rights around Provence remain embedded in complex dynastic relationships. Local cooperation remains necessary even after diplomatic agreement.

[Income and the costs of acquisition] Royal estates, markets, port charges, salt-related revenues, and obligations imposed on Jewish and Muslim communities provide differentiated resources. Exemptions and payment conditions depend on particular privileges; neither uniform cargo duties nor identical regional assemblies should be assumed. Newly conquered land brings garrisoning, settlement, litigation, and irrigation costs as well as income. Grants to nobles or religious institutions may reduce what the monarch directly receives. Merchants can support safe trade while opposing prolonged requisition of ships without dependable compensation. Muslim cultivators who lose livestock, water access, or harvests cannot supply the same rents in the following season. The Barcelona maritime ordinances of 1258 regulate cargo, freight, and obligations between crews and merchants, showing that commercial security also requires enforceable agreements. Fiscal strength rests on the settlement after conquest, not simply a larger outline on a map.

[Service and combined operations] Noble cavalry, town forces, crossbowmen, and lightly equipped frontier fighters perform different tasks and serve under varying obligations. Their duties and terms of service differ, requiring separate arrangements for a prolonged campaign. The Majorcan and Valencian campaigns have provided experience of sea transport, landing, and siege, but hired merchant vessels still require sailors and supplies. Light troops familiar with rough ground are useful without every almogavar being capable of destroying armored cavalry in open battle. Horsemen likewise need suitable terrain and supporting troops. Taking a fortress requires engineering, blockade, and dependable provisioning; defending a port requires cooperation from townspeople and mariners. Simultaneous inland and maritime wars can rapidly create demands for coordination and cash beyond the resources of a single feudal summons.

[Treaties, frontiers, and competing merchants] The Almizra settlement of 1244 defines spheres of expansion between Aragon and Castile. The Valencian southern frontier and Murcia must be handled against these commitments; marriage ties remove neither territorial competition nor the possibility of accommodation. Italian and Provençal merchants can be competitors, carriers, creditors, and customers at once. Commercial rivalry does not make permanent war along every route inevitable. Northern agreement provides time for consolidation, while the south remains vulnerable to resistance among conquered populations and armed frontier activity. Interests around Sicily and Sardinia must be weighed against available shipping, local cooperation, and the risk of entanglement with France, the papacy, and maritime powers. Present interests are the security of existing ports, the reliability of income, and the practical observance of agreements.

[Internal bargaining and usable alternatives] Inland nobles expect land and jurisdiction from conquest, while urban merchants emphasize predictable exchange. Their interests overlap, but they can disagree over where money and service are spent. Valencian legal and settlement arrangements also affect established feudatories and new inhabitants differently. Provision for the king's sons is a dynastic question, requiring agreement among relatives and territories with competing expectations of continuity. Treating one territory as an inexhaustible source of money for another's campaigns weakens the union. When resources or obedience falter, suspending an expedition, confirming local rights, repairing channels, and renegotiating commercial terms remain practical choices. The loss of immediate prestige may be smaller than the cost of destroying the allegiance and revenue on which the common crown depends.
armenia:
[Mountains, plain, and maritime connections] Cilicia lies between the Taurus Mountains and the northeastern Mediterranean. Tarsus and the castles of Sis, Lampron, Corycus, and Sarvandikar anchor the royal possessions. Mountain routes connect the coast with the Anatolian plateau, while the plain supports cultivation and the coastal trading network reaches toward Ayas. The Seyhan and Ceyhan are separate rivers, rather than a single confluence supporting every settlement. Grain, pasture, timber, and access to markets matter alongside imported luxuries. Roads toward Antioch and Aleppo make prosperity dependent on security beyond the kingdom's walls. A castle can close a pass, but it cannot by itself guarantee merchants a safe journey through another ruler's territory.

[A crown sustained by marriage and recognition] The coronation of Levon in 1198 gave the Rubenid principality royal standing. Hethum I's marriage to Queen Isabella in 1226 established Hethumid rule through the existing succession, rather than making him simply another Rubenid king. Coronation, dynastic relationships, and recognition by important neighbors support royal legitimacy, but they do not eliminate bargaining with powerful lordships. Armenian ecclesiastical institutions retain their own traditions. Connections with Latin rulers and the papacy provide diplomatic opportunities without establishing an uncontested union of churches. The king must distinguish cooperation abroad from the religious concessions that bishops, monasteries, and subjects will accept at home; demanding both together risks losing support for an otherwise useful alliance.

[Customs, estates, and the cost of protection] Royal estates, agricultural dues, and commercial receipts provide different kinds of resources. Merchant privileges require agreements about access, charges, and protection; the value of goods passing through a harbor is not the king's disposable income. Mountain transport adds costs before supplies reach a garrison. Relations with the Mongol court require expensive journeys, gifts, and military commitments, even when protection benefits the kingdom. Religious exemptions and lordly rights also limit what officials can collect. The treasury therefore depends on keeping cultivation and trade functioning, rather than repeatedly extracting the same reserves. Concessions that attract traders can improve receipts over time, while arbitrary demands may divert traffic to competing ports and impoverish the routes inland.

[Fortresses and a limited field army] Lordly cavalry, household forces, local fighting men, and castle garrisons give Cilicia several military instruments. Their effectiveness depends on terrain and supply. A mounted contingent can accompany an ally into an open campaign, whereas a pass requires watchmen, stores, water, and a commander who will remain loyal during isolation. The same men and animals cannot indefinitely defend every fortress and serve abroad. Agreements over the length of service and provision of fodder matter as much as declarations of alliance. The king's strategic advantage lies in making an attacker traverse controlled approaches, while preserving a mobile reserve. Sending the entire available force south would expose the cultivated plain and leave the government dependent on another army's priorities.

[Mongol commitments and uncertain southern developments] Smbat's mission in 1247 and Hethum's own journey to the great khan in 1254 established a relationship of submission and protection. The fall of Baghdad in 1258 demonstrates the scale of Mongol power and raises the stakes of every regional choice. It does not settle the outcome of a Syrian campaign or guarantee safety from Egypt. Neighboring towns answer to different authorities, whose garrisons and agreements determine access. Antioch offers kinship and political connections, while the Sultanate of Rum remains a neighboring concern under Mongol pressure. Each relationship involves separate obligations. The king must weigh each commitment against the protection his partners can presently provide.

[Different constituencies and a defensible fallback] Castle lords weigh service against security of their estates; churchmen weigh diplomatic benefits against protection of their institutions; merchants need predictable passage and charges. These interests overlap without forming two neatly organized parties for Mongolia and Europe. The crown must win cooperation on particular obligations and avoid treating disagreement as automatic treason. A successful distant campaign may still impose costs at home if labor, horses, and grain are taken from productive districts. When allies cannot offer timely help, fortified withdrawal, restricted commitments, negotiation, and ransom remain practical tools. Preserving people, accessible markets, and the willingness of local lords to cooperate provides a basis for recovery; prestige alone cannot replace them.
bohemia:
[Geography and economic connections] Bohemian royal holdings include Prague, Brno, Pilsen, Ostrava, and fortresses including Křivoklát, anchoring it in the upper Elbe and Vltava basin and Moravia. Ottokar II possesses strong Austrian claims through noble acceptance and marriage, but Vienna remains tied to imperial interests beyond his immediate command. Prague joins a royal seat to crossings, workshops, and markets; Brno connects the heartland toward the Danube. Mountain borders impede invasion but also concentrate merchants, salt supplies, and armies into vulnerable corridors. Agriculture, timber, livestock, urban exchange, and mining all sustain royal power. Jihlava already matters as a mining town. Miners require skilled labor, timber, and dependable trading connections; the crown needs to protect working mines and minting rights while honoring the terms that draw experienced operators. Maintaining bridges and safe roads is therefore as consequential as possessing an impressive cavalry following. A southern expedition cannot live on the prestige of its distant king.

[Dynastic authority and disputed inheritance] The Bohemian crown belongs to the Přemyslid dynasty and its hereditary standing was confirmed by the Golden Bull of 1212. Ottokar succeeded Wenceslaus I in 1253, having already obtained Austrian aristocratic acceptance in 1251. His marriage in 1252 to Margaret of Babenberg supplied an additional basis for holding Austria after the extinction of its ruling male line. Neither marriage nor local acclamation settles every rival claim. The arrangement reached in 1254 recognized most of Austria under Ottokar while assigning much of Styria to Hungary. Styria is consequently an unresolved struggle in 1259, not an accomplished Bohemian annexation. Imperial recognition, provincial cooperation, and the capacity to defend possession remain separate necessities. No charter makes the ruler immune to a competing interpretation backed by soldiers.

[Revenue and the price of privileges] Estate income, market and road dues, urban obligations, mining rights, and minting provide several streams of resources. Silver deposits are not immediately spendable wages: extraction requires labor, timber, drainage, and functioning exchange. Civic privileges can attract settlement and predictable rents, but they also limit the ability of neighboring magnates to divert urban business into their jurisdictions. Ottokar's protection of Jewish inhabitants in 1254 demonstrates the crown's willingness to place vulnerable communities under royal safeguards; it does not remove their exposure to fiscal demands or local hostility. Austrian revenues likewise cannot all be transferred to Prague at will. Churches, nobles, and towns retain claims requiring negotiation. Long-term compliance may be worth more than an exceptionally large collection followed by resistance. Specific charters divide what the crown may collect from revenues retained locally or granted to supporters.

[Military resources and operational limits] Household followers, aristocratic cavalry, locally mobilized infantry, and fortress garrisons form the military foundation. Armored horsemen can deliver decisive force on suitable ground, but movement between provinces depends on crossings, fodder, wagons, and defended staging points. Towns may owe guard and transport duties without constituting a uniform national standing army. Ottokar's Prussian expedition of 1254–1255 enhanced his crusading standing and his relationship with the Teutonic Order; it does not provide a permanently available reserve for every Danubian campaign. Against Hungary and its mobile mounted forces, scouting and protection of the supply route matter alongside shock action. Extended service demands compensation and agreement, while a failed campaign may consume horses and equipment that cannot quickly be replaced.

[Foreign competition and priorities] Béla IV of Hungary and his son Stephen retain a direct interest in Styria, and neighboring German princes also watch the changing Danubian balance. The loyalties of provincial lords may change a frontier faster than one successful battle. The competing royal claims of Richard of Cornwall and Alfonso of Castile mean that imperial arbitration is itself politically divided. Ottokar can bargain for recognition and exploit disagreements, but the kingship of the Romans is not an unclaimed prize awaiting the richest bidder. The immediate priority is a defensible connection between existing possessions before assuming additional burdens. Recognition can change with military power and bargains, so diplomatic success still requires defensible positions. Diplomacy must therefore retain usable alternatives rather than make every claim a test of personal honor.

[Internal tensions and a viable retreat] Town foundation, immigration, and new settlement can enlarge the revenue base while threatening established noble courts and local influence. Language differences intersect with land boundaries and competing privileges, so allies and opponents need not follow one linguistic divide. Austrian lords may welcome a powerful protector while resisting disregard for their customs. The royal marriage has not produced an accepted male heir, making succession and marital legitimacy sensitive while the marriage supporting Austrian rights also requires continued noble and ecclesiastical acceptance. The central danger is overcommitment: aristocratic service, urban subsidies, and provincial obedience are not inexhaustible resources. If the southern contest deteriorates, a limited truce, renewed confirmation of local rights, and preservation of the main roads offer a better foundation for recovery than another campaign financed against uncertain future income.
bosnia:
[Valleys and the royal possessions] Bosnia's mountains divide settlement into corridors whose communications depend on river valleys, passes, and pack transport. The ban holds Borać, Kamen, Banja Luka, and western positions labeled Zagrab and Laibach. Their dispersed position makes local cooperation essential to collecting dues and providing relief. Movement between them requires accessible routes and cooperation from local holders. Agriculture and livestock support communities that cannot always send surplus elsewhere quickly. Connections toward the Adriatic give inland producers access to wider markets, but access is different from ownership of coastal towns. A defensible position must therefore be judged by its stores and communications as well as the apparent extent of the ruler's territory.

[The ban and competing forms of recognition] The succession after Matej Ninoslav leaves competing claims to authority and regional influence. Prijezda draws support from Hungarian connections and Catholic affiliation while local holders seek to retain autonomy and inherited rights. The ban must make authority effective through local agreements. Hungarian kingship, papal claims, and Bosnian lordship offer different tests of legitimate government. Recognition from abroad can strengthen a ban's standing but does not automatically deliver local obedience or taxes. Agreements with influential families must make authority practical: who judges disputes, who confirms estates, and what assistance is owed when an army approaches are more immediate questions than an abstract claim to unlimited sovereignty.

[Trade and revenues that can actually be collected] Estates, herding, local markets, and charges on movement offer a mixture of produce and money. Trade toward Ragusa and other Dalmatian centers depends on credible protection and settlement of disputes involving travelers. Mining receipts depend on workings that can be supplied, operated, and brought within the ruler's collection rights. Nor does a claim to jurisdiction mean that every due reaches the ban: local lords and religious institutions hold rights of their own. Maintaining roads and resolving competing exactions can make commerce more dependable. Repeated extraordinary demands may instead encourage merchants to avoid a route and communities to conceal supplies, leaving the ruler with nominal rights but fewer usable resources when military pressure arrives.

[Military cooperation in difficult terrain] The ban's immediate following and the forces of local lordships provide the foundation for defense. Their obligations are personal and territorial; there is no reason to invent a uniform standing army or a standardized national military budget. Mountains can slow an invader, but they also constrain relief columns and the movement of food. Fortifications require stores, watchmen, and arrangements for replacing men who must return to their households. A small force familiar with an approach can delay a stronger enemy, provided neighboring holders cooperate. Attempting distant operations on several fronts would spread these advantages thinly. The military problem is to preserve connected defensive positions and reliable local assistance, rather than merely to maximize the number of men nominally summoned.

[Hungary, Serbia, and the coastal connections] Hungarian intervention, Serbian power, and disputes involving Hum create pressures from different directions. Dalmatian towns offer commercial contacts without necessarily sharing the ban's military objectives. Earlier crusading claims against Bosnia show how religious accusations can support external intervention, although the details of particular campaigns and territorial control remain disputed. Neighboring claims remain contested where their holders lack local recognition or garrisons. Diplomacy must work with the forces and support presently available. Envoys, recognition of limited obligations, and commercial guarantees can reduce isolation. Their value depends on terms local supporters can honor, since promises of unrestricted service or sweeping religious change may destroy the cooperation needed to implement any foreign agreement.

[Religious differences and the costs of consolidation] Religious accusations concerning the Bosnian Church intersect with outside intervention, while local worship, Catholic connections, and family loyalties do not coincide neatly. Catholic connections, local religious practices, and family loyalties interact in political life. Measures intended to satisfy an outside patron can alienate the people who maintain estates and defend passes. Conversely, protecting local interests without any diplomatic explanation may invite renewed accusations and intervention. The ban needs specific compromises and trusted intermediaries rather than a claim that every dispute has already been settled. In a serious crisis, preserving communities, communications, and a guaranteed truce offers a firmer basis for continued rule than enforcing uniformity at the cost of a combined foreign and domestic war.
brittany:
[A peninsula of ports and corridors] Brittany projects into the Atlantic and the Channel. Roads linking Rennes, the Nantes direction, and western ports matter more than a neat frontier; castles and river mouths shape movement. Quimper, Rennes, and several castles require garrisons and protected communications. Fish, salt, grain, timber, and port exchange support different districts. Sea distance creates seasonal and weather risks: a port can widen options without making supply automatic. Inland roads and river crossings must still be protected before a coastal privilege becomes usable income.

[Ducal authority and lordly custom] Ducal legitimacy rests on succession, marriage, feudal custom, and recognition by the French crown, which do not always point in the same direction. John I must negotiate courts, service, and castle duties with his lords. Lords retain bargaining space over courts, service, and inherited rights. A confirmation can secure immediate loyalty but narrow future revenue; a new levy may strengthen a garrison while teaching the same lord to resist the next demand. Political control is therefore assembled through particular agreements rather than assumed from the title alone.

[Estates and port revenue] Rents, market dues, salt, and port transit provide collectable resources, but castles and shipping consume them. Foreign merchants need clear terms for protection and charges; arbitrary demands can redirect traffic toward Normandy or Ireland. Ecclesiastical and lordly exemptions limit ready cash. Commercial receipts depend on the cargoes, crews, and markets that can presently use the ports. A stable harbor may be more valuable than a higher one-time charge when the duke needs repeated access to food, timber, and credit.

[Knights, castles, and ships] The military mix consists of ducal retainers, lordly knights, town contingents, and castle garrisons; there is no fixed national army ready for every expedition. Shipping can move limited supplies quickly, but weather, crews, and control of harbors constrain its reliability. Castle defense and field operations need separate allocations. A continental war that removes the men guarding the peninsula can turn a diplomatic success into a domestic crisis.

[Choices between England and France] French recognition in the west and English connections across the Channel, Ireland, and Aquitaine can each serve as leverage. English and French negotiations concern old claims and Aquitanian obligations, leaving Breton interests in passage, trade, and service to be negotiated. Terms over trade, passage, and service remain available for bargaining. The duke should trade particular access, neutrality, or service for a particular guarantee, always keeping a route back to local autonomy.

[Local identity and a fallback] Families, churches, ports, and rural communities have different interests. Simultaneous taxation, levies, and interference in local courts can turn groups that might cooperate into a coalition against the duke. Protect food routes, ports, and castles first. If necessary, request French arbitration or open trade to English merchants; if both are unreliable, contract to the peninsula's core and rebuild order through marriage and negotiated rights. The long-term asset is a Breton authority that can still make agreements, not a spectacular campaign that leaves no money or trusted lords.
bulgaria:
[Danube, mountains, and dispersed holdings] The Bulgarian towns, castles, and river ports stretch across the lower Danube, Balkan approaches, and Black Sea direction, making relief expensive. Sofia, Kilia, Giurgiu, Varna, and other positions have distinct supply routes and defensive burdens. Rivers are both supply routes and defensive lines. Black Sea revenue depends on ships and security, while mountain roads slow both invaders and royal relief. A court at Tarnovo must ration attention among corridors rather than imagine that a single victory secures the entire frontier.

[The practical basis of the crown] Constantine Tih became emperor in 1257 after succession struggles had weakened central authority. His marriage to Irene Laskarina connected him to the Nicaean imperial house, but marriage did not erase the boyars' power. Orthodox institutions, aristocratic councils, and towns all form part of the regime's social base. The crown must keep converting recognition into protection and a workable distribution of offices, lands, and obligations. A title alone cannot restore the authority lost during years of short reigns and territorial reversals.

[Tribute, estates, and ports] Royal resources include estate produce, market dues, and customs at river and sea ports; the usable amount changes with local retention, war, and road security. Mongol tribute is a real cost. Black Sea trade and minerals are not unlimited cash. Ecclesiastical property and lordly privileges limit taxation. When receipts fall, reducing a distant expedition is more sustainable than exhausting border villages and losing the producers who feed the garrisons.

[Cavalry, local forces, and defense] Boyar cavalry can maneuver on the plains, while troops at mountains and crossings delay an advance. Town militias and local forces serve for different periods. A steppe threat requires scouting, control of crossings, and stocked depots rather than only a decisive heavy-cavalry battle. Multiple fronts expose Tarnovo and the dispersed castles. Service terms must respect harvests if the army is to return with food and political support.

[Mongols, Nicaea, and northern pressure] Tribute and steppe pressure impose a short-term submission cost. Nicaean power, moving toward Constantinople, contests influence in Thrace and the straits. Hungary and Serbia can exploit Bulgarian weakness. The court needs separate agreements to prevent external pressure and local disputes over taxation and service from escalating together. The court should seek time, information, and separate bargains rather than choose a single permanent alignment before the balance is clear.

[Boyar bargaining and a fallback] After succession contests, boyars need estates, offices, and a credible share of gains; the church needs protection and exemptions; towns need stable markets. A king who fights on every frontier invites one of these groups to back a rival. Use local recognition, marriage, and truces to preserve the core. If the treasury breaks, abandon isolated positions rather than the Tarnovo–Danube food connection and royal legitimacy. A smaller realm that can pay guards and negotiate is a better recovery base than a wide map held only by promises.
castile:
[Plateau, roads, and contested boundaries] Castilian holdings include Toledo, León, Santiago, Badajoz, and several fortresses, linking the Meseta to western river valleys. Grain, livestock, hides, and urban exchange move along routes constrained by mountains, drought, and successive charges. Extensive pasture does not make campaign provisions instantly available. Ferdinand III's conquests provide claims in the south, but Seville is presently controlled by Granada. Royal claims do not supply its customs, officials, or garrison, and making them effective would require diplomatic and military commitments. Northern shipping and wool exchange form part of the regional background, but shipping still requires specific agreements with port authorities and owners. Logistics must follow the positions actually available on this campaign map.

[The united crown and written law] Castile and León came under one monarch in 1230 without erasing their local institutions. Alfonso, reigning since 1252, combines dynastic conquest with legal and learned patronage. The Fuero Real of 1255 and the developing law-book enterprise touch municipal customs and aristocratic jurisdictions. The developing Siete Partidas express a common legal ambition while local judgment still encounters older rights and resistance. In 1257 some German electors supported Alfonso as king of the Romans while others backed Richard of Cornwall. The disputed title is not a completed imperial coronation and does not deliver German taxes or troops to Toledo. Royal authority still depends on persuading people who recognize quite different limits on obedience.

[Multiple resources and competing commitments] Estate dues, market and transit charges, pastoral revenues, community obligations, and negotiated grants supply different resources. Town privileges, ecclesiastical rights, and great landed lordships restrict direct royal access. Pastoral owners use local agreements, routes, and privileges, with grazing claims competing against cultivation. Wool income is divided among owners and collecting authorities; additional royal returns require cooperation rather than an assumption that every transaction belongs to the crown. Southern land distribution, settlement, and defense consume resources alongside the returns of conquest. Muslim cultivators require working irrigation, livestock, and subsistence to keep producing rents. The imperial candidacy entails embassies, gifts, and financial promises. Domestic interests can consequently ask whether those payments improve their security or chiefly purchase a distant royal dignity.

[Service, military orders, and siege warfare] Magnates' mounted followers, the royal household, municipal knights, and military orders provide distinct forces rather than one professional army on a common pay scale. Santiago, Calatrava, and Alcántara possess organizational and territorial interests requiring coordination with the crown. Municipal mounted service is connected to privileges and the means to maintain a horse and equipment. Cavalry assists reconnaissance, raiding, and battle on suitable terrain; taking fortified mountain positions requires infantry, engineering, blockade, and transport. Excessive agricultural levies damage the harvest that later supports campaigning, and extended service demands compensation. Expected booty cannot already pay for an uncommenced siege. A realistic strategy respects seasonal provisioning and the actual roads linking the army to its supporters.

[Southern settlements and neighboring crowns] The Jaén arrangement of 1246 binds Muhammad I to Castilian overlordship and tribute in exchange for a truce and continued possession elsewhere. Suzerainty, payment, and physical occupation remain different things. The Alcaraz agreement of 1243 similarly preserves local arrangements in Murcia alongside Castilian military involvement. Aragon refers to the Almizra settlement of 1244 when defending its sphere of expansion; Portugal maintains separate claims over the Algarve. Marriage helps negotiations without extinguishing all competing rights. North African rulers also have their own conflicts: the scale of help available to Granada depends on competing interests, shipping, and commitments at home. Maintaining tribute and peace may provide more dependable returns than an expensive siege.

[Domestic tensions and competing rights] Magnates resist lost jurisdiction and independent revenues; towns may welcome royal protection while rejecting additional taxes; conquered communities defend land, worship, and personal safety. They are not one unified opposition. Learned patronage and crusading language do not demonstrate consent to every fiscal measure. The prospects of royal children and relatives affect expectations of offices and property, while magnates can express dynastic loyalty alongside insistence on their own rights. The immediate danger is pressing imperial ambitions, legal intervention, and southern campaigning beyond the capacity of several constituencies at once. Reducing distant diplomatic expenditure, confirming selected privileges, and renewing frontier truces provide alternatives. Actual strongholds and dependable income should be preserved before adding new commitments. Royal strength depends on sustaining obligations across varied territories, not merely multiplying titles on parchment.
chernigov:
[Rivers and dispersed towns] The Desna and Seym basins connect Chernigov, Novgorod-Seversky, Kursk, and Starodub. Yelets, Homiel, Novosil, and other holdings extend the defensive problem across several approaches. Forests, crossings, and roads determine which garrisons can assist one another. The southern edge faces the steppe, while woodland does not make a settlement immune to attack. Winter conditions may open routes that are difficult in another season. Food and transport therefore need preparation before a warning arrives, rather than being assumed from the map's broad forest cover.

[Olgovichi patrimony and recognition] Family branches and inherited domains sustain princely legitimacy. Earlier contests for Kyiv or Galicia do not establish present control of their revenues. The Mongol capture of Chernigov in 1239 forms part of the background to recovery. The damage of conquest leaves the recovery of people, defenses, and revenue closely tied to recognition of inherited rights. Family precedence, possession, and recognition by superior powers can support different candidates. Securing a workable agreement among relatives is therefore an immediate political task, not a detail resolved by reciting an ancient genealogy.

[Recovery and tributary burdens] Agriculture, livestock, markets, and river crossings supply the court, but losses of people, transport costs, and tribute reduce the usable surplus. Protecting church and monastic estates supports religious legitimacy while limiting extraordinary collection. Reopening fields, encouraging settlement, and restraining repeated demands along a route can enlarge future receipts. Immediate extraction cannot substitute for that recovery. The ruler must distinguish what a district produces from what can reach the treasury after local obligations, military needs, and payment to the khan. An unrealistic assessment risks driving cultivators away and leaving both the garrison and the tribute collector without resources.

[Defense with limited forces] Princely retainers, local warriors, and town garrisons can defend crossings and earth-and-timber works. They cannot sustain an unrestricted pursuit of steppe cavalry. Warning, reconnaissance, and avoiding encirclement matter more than a battle chosen for the prestige of the old capital. Local holders also have patrimonies to defend. Service beyond their district requires agreement over duration and supply, since an expedition can leave northern nodes exposed. The useful aim is to preserve a network that can warn, shelter, and reinforce, with a reserve capable of moving between threatened positions.

[The khan and neighboring Rus lands] Recognition, tribute, and relations among Rus families intersect without creating a single permanent alliance. Smolensk, Kyiv, Ryazan, and the northeastern princes may cooperate on one issue and compete on another. Embassies, marriages, safe passage, and trading arrangements should therefore be negotiated separately. A concession to the khan may prevent an immediate attack without settling succession at home. Neighboring powers and family relationships remain changeable, making several channels of cooperation valuable. Policy must work with the present holdings and the support that neighboring rulers can actually deliver.

[Family costs and a fallback] Appanages give relatives a stake in survival but require repeated bargaining over taxes and service. Church protection, functioning markets, and guaranteed family arrangements can reduce the cost of that bargaining. If tribute and military demands exceed capacity, seek time and a limited withdrawal, move food and livestock north, and retain connected towns. Maintaining people, routes, and credit provides a basis for renewed strength. An ambitious title acquired without these resources would add another obligation while weakening the patrimony that made the claim possible.
crusaderstates:
[Coast and inland holdings] Jerusalem, Kerak, Arish, and the other inland positions depend on their own routes and defenders. Acre, Tripoli, and Antioch each have distinct hinterlands, ports, and mountain defenses. Shipping can bring grain, but seasons, merchants, and enemy fleets determine whether it arrives. Possessing a town is different from safely collecting the produce of every surrounding village. The government must therefore consider access between a port and its fortresses, the security of storage, and the costs of escorting supplies. Inland prestige cannot compensate for a harbor unable to provision its defenders.

[Several forms of legitimate authority] Claims to Jerusalem's crown, actual regency, connections with Cyprus, and the local rights of Antioch and Tripoli coexist. Baronial courts and military orders maintain privileges of their own. Naming one crusader king does not establish centralized command over them. An agreement to surrender a right, pay for a fleet, or undertake a campaign requires consent from the holders affected. Lords may disagree about regency and service even when they recognize the same crown. Dynastic claims provide a language for bargaining; they do not automatically supply money or obedience from each coastal polity.

[Ports, quarters, and privileges] Customs, markets, estates, and contributions from abroad support defense, while Italian trading privileges and the property of military orders restrict the royal share. The value of merchandise passing through a harbor is not its tax yield. European assistance is neither regular nor guaranteed. Violence among port quarters damages warehouses, transport, and credit before it harms an external enemy. Negotiated protection and dependable courts can therefore improve finances more effectively than a higher nominal charge. Every concession should be assessed against what it secures in ships, stores, or sustained access, rather than presented as either unlimited prosperity or simple surrender.

[Orders, fortresses, and sailing schedules] Knights, military orders, mercenaries, and town guards perform different tasks. A major fortress still needs water, food, and replaceable defenders. Field cavalry cannot solve a blockade, while ships cannot indefinitely maintain every isolated inland castle. The service period of visiting troops and the timetable of return voyages constrain campaign choices. A government must avoid an operation whose initial strength disappears when supporters sail home. Holding a connected coastal position, with a manageable number of supplied forts, can be militarily more valuable than defending every historic claim at equal cost.

[Saint Sabas and neighboring powers] The War of Saint Sabas, beginning in 1256, draws merchant rivalries, lords, and military orders into Acre's politics. The naval fighting and Genoese setback in 1258 have already altered the terms of cooperation. Mongol movement west and Egyptian military power create serious pressure, but they do not establish the outcome of a Syrian campaign. The allegiance of Syrian towns and the arrival of relief remain uncertain. Different Latin governments may reasonably make different bargains. One ruler's submission or truce must be distinguished from a promise made by every neighboring lord or port.

[Cooperation and withdrawal] Churches, lords, residents, and merchants bear different losses. Requisitioning shipping may save one campaign while damaging the next season's supply. Guarantees over customs, passage, and the division of garrison costs can reduce division without pretending every interest is identical. In crisis, preserve ports that can receive ships, move stores and dependants, and negotiate ransom or peace where necessary. A reliable sea connection sustains a community and a future military option. An uncompromising declaration against every neighbor may instead leave a celebrated fortress without the food, sailors, or partners needed to remain inhabited.
denmark:
[Islands and sea routes] Jutland, Zealand, and Scania are connected by shipping among Ribe, Aalborg, Roskilde, Lund, and Helsingborg. Weather, crossings, and available crews determine whether one district can assist another. A land garrison cannot substitute for transport across the straits. Coastal fisheries and local hinterlands generate income, but possession of a coast does not establish a universal tax on every passing vessel. The crown needs dependable points of embarkation, stocked islands, and cooperation from shipowners before claiming strategic control of the surrounding water.

[Succession and recognition] Christopher I became king in 1252. Royal branches and nobles retain different expectations of succession, and recognition for his son depends on cooperation with churchmen and local holders. Rival royal branches and noble recognition remain central to legitimacy, so possession of the royal title does not remove the need to negotiate with families holding regional power.

[Local revenue and merchants] Royal estates, markets, fisheries, and particular port charges support the court alongside the rights of churches and nobles. Port charges require local rights and merchant agreements; receipts depend on goods actually reaching the harbor. Relations with Lübeck and other towns can provide ships and goods through particular commercial agreements. Merchant privileges should specify obligations and protections. Raising a charge without protecting access may divert trade and deprive the crown of the transport it needs more urgently than the disputed payment.

[Ships and regional forces] Royal households, nobles, and towns provide different ships and fighting men. A crossing requires agreements about service, equipment, and provisions. Taking a coastal position does not automatically secure its hinterland. Maritime defense, royal castles, and the Schleswig frontier compete for the same resources. Excessive requisition of vessels and food can damage both commerce and fishing, weakening the economic base that supports the fleet. Local cooperation is therefore a military requirement rather than a concession that can safely be postponed until after victory.

[Church conflict and southern disputes] Archbishop Jakob Erlandsen's conflict with the crown concerns ecclesiastical rights and recognition of succession. The descendants of Abel in Schleswig pursue a different dynastic interest, while Rügen and north German connections can complicate intervention. These are related pressures, not one organized national enemy. If ecclesiastical conflict and southern dynastic disputes worsen together, the court may struggle to maintain communication across the water. Mediation can reduce one dispute even if another remains unresolved.

[Domestic cost and fallback] Property taxation has provoked resistance, and ecclesiastical conflict can obstruct local implementation. Nobles, bishops, and merchants need agreements whose particular obligations they can fulfill. If the crown cannot defend both the southern frontier and sea routes, truces, arbitration, and limited privileges can preserve island communications. The durable advantage lies in crews who can be mobilized again, stores that can be replenished, and recognition that survives a compromise. A distant victory bought by exhausting all three may weaken rather than secure the monarchy.
england:
[Geography] London and the Thames connect grain, wool, and overseas commerce. The crown also holds Bordeaux, Dublin, Waterford, and northern castles. Dover, Chester, and York have different supply requirements. Sea crossings, the Welsh marches, and the northern border cannot all be defended by the same force; protecting a port is useful only if ships and an inland route remain available.

[Legitimacy] Henry III has ruled since 1216. Reissues of Magna Carta form a tradition of restraint and negotiation between kingship and the political community. The reforms of Oxford in 1258 require supervision of offices and regular councils. Their meaning remains disputed; they establish neither universal democracy nor the disappearance of royal authority.

[Revenue] Estate rents, judicial receipts, scutage, privileges, and negotiated grants support the court. The Sicilian project, patronage, and debt have damaged credit. Wool exports matter, while royal receipts depend on existing collection rights and negotiated grants. The value of traded wool greatly exceeds the share that can reach the royal treasury.

[Forces] Royal households, noble cavalry, paid troops, and local levies have different terms of service. Castles, fodder, shipping, and wages determine endurance. Archers require training, arrows, suitable terrain, and support from other troops. Sustaining Gascony reduces the money and troops available at home, making coordination with local supporters essential.

[Diplomacy] France, Wales, Scotland, colonial Ireland, and the papacy present different problems. Paris negotiations concern territorial claims and homage, while proposals for judicial reform require agreement among king, magnates, and local knights.

[Domestic bargains] Montfort, the Gloucester interest, local knights, and the royal household form changing coalitions. Their support can change as offices, reform, and jurisdiction are negotiated. Credible accounts, limited reform, and guaranteed truces can preserve kingship while reducing war costs. After a setback, hold connected castles and shipping rather than expand opposition through indiscriminate confiscation.
france:
[Geography] The Seine, Loire, and Paris basin form the royal transport core. The crown also holds Toulouse, Marseille, Lyon, and positions toward Flanders. Distant towns do not provide an unlimited common treasury. North-south roads, crossings, and markets require separate protection, and frontier claims must be distinguished from the holdings actually available for collection.

[Legitimacy] Capetian succession, ecclesiastical coronation, and feudal relationships support Louis IX. Appeals and royal justice extend influence through local implementation. Royal action depends on officers and cooperation from holders of local rights. Royal appanages and great lordships hold real rights, so an increase in royal authority requires officers, negotiated cooperation, and decisions that communities will accept.

[Revenue] Estates, markets, transit, and judicial receipts supply usable resources, while war and ransom reduce the balance. Crusading taxation and ecclesiastical assistance are not annual automatic grants. Royal, appanage, and local revenues must be distinguished. Protecting exchange and credit sustains repeated collection more effectively than treating every emergency as permission to demand the same reserves again.

[Forces] Feudal cavalry, household troops, paid forces, and town obligations complement one another. Sieges need transport, wages, and equipment. An eastern expedition competes with home defense for ships, money, and noble service. Losses in the Seventh Crusade encourage renewed scrutiny of supplies, partners, and the burdens of an expedition.

[Diplomacy] The English king's independent crown coexists with his feudal position in Aquitaine. Paris negotiations over concessions, homage, and older claims require separate confirmation and implementation. Iberian kings, the papacy, imperial princes, and maritime merchants offer different instruments. The durability of a settlement depends on how both crowns address local rights and disputes.

[Costs and fallback] Judicial expansion can reduce local income, religious policies can harm protected groups and credit, and expeditions increase burdens. Arbitration, privileges, and bounded homage can preserve a frontier without continuous campaigning. Defend the existing towns first. The prestige of universal justice cannot finance intervention in every neighboring dispute or replace the support of people who bear the costs.
gaelic:
[Dispersed territories] Galway, Kinbane, and Maine connect different local networks rather than one continuous administrative district. Rivers, mountains, woods, and pasture determine the routes of assembly and raiding. Coastal exchange depends on those who hold the ports. English possession of Dublin and Waterford does not establish control of the entire island, while native lands also contain complicated rights and rival claims. Any campaign must identify where its people, food, and animals can gather and which intervening rulers will permit passage.

[Kingship and kindreds] Gaelic titles, dynastic succession, and local recognition do not describe a single feudal monarchy. A claim to high kingship particularly requires practical cooperation. Brian O'Neill has sought cooperation among rulers, whose contributions still depend on local consent. Each kindred weighs the protection and benefits offered by cooperation. Recognition must be translated into a stated contribution or agreement; an honorific title alone does not supply warriors from a competing kindred.

[Herds and tribute] Livestock, cultivation, tribute, rents, and markets support local rule. Raiding can produce spoils but also invites retaliation and damages production. Treating every successful raid as fiscal growth ignores hunger, displacement, and the need to rebuild herds. Churches and urban exchange offer mediation and access to money. A ruler must distinguish resources taken once from an income that supporters can provide again. Preserving animals and the people who tend them can be strategically more useful than accumulating goods that cannot feed a continuing host.

[Local forces and movement] Kindred forces, mounted followers, and infantry assemble through local obligations with different equipment and expectations. Keeping them together is difficult without food and an agreed purpose. Woods, narrow approaches, and crossings can restrict armored cavalry but do not make a district invulnerable. Operations should concern identifiable castles, herds, and routes. Different followings require their own arrangements for service and supply. The duration of a host and the arrangements for sharing gains matter as much as the enthusiasm accompanying its assembly.

[Colonial lords and neighbors] The English crown, Anglo-Norman families, native kings, and connections with Scotland and Wales offer different opportunities. Colonial lords are not always a single obedient royal army, and native families are not automatically allies. A trading truce in one district may coexist with conflict elsewhere. A truce in one district does not guarantee peace elsewhere. The useful diplomatic task is to identify who can grant passage, restrain a raid, or recognize a claim and what return that actor requires.

[Coalition costs and recovery] A common cause that cannot divide gains, confirm land, or address succession can intensify suspicion among allies. Local autonomy, ransom, and ecclesiastical mediation can sustain cooperation without demanding permanent submission. After a setback, preserve core pasture and people and end an expedition the country cannot supply. A local truce does not mean the entire island has yielded. Rebuilding communities, herds, and confidence gives rulers a basis for another agreement; a title defended at their expense may leave nobody willing to answer the next summons.
galicia:
[Geography] Halych, Volodymyr, Lutsk, and Brest connect routes toward Poland, the Carpathians, and the steppe. The Dniester, Bug, and overland roads have different transport limits. Access to a route does not make all Black Sea commerce taxable by the prince, and scattered castles require local stores as well as movement between larger towns.

[Legitimacy] Daniel and his brother Vasylko consolidated Romanovichi territory, with the victory at Yaroslav in 1245 forming important background. The crown received in 1253 strengthens foreign recognition without abolishing Orthodox institutions or Mongol influence. Royal recognition must still be translated into support among towns, boyars, and relatives.

[Revenue] Town rebuilding, settlers, craftsmen, estates, and exchange can restore resources after conquest. Privileges attract people while limiting arbitrary demands. Boyars and churches retain shares of income. Fortification and tribute compete for surplus, and a royal crown does not guarantee European money or the supplies required to maintain new defenses.

[Forces] Princely followers, boyar cavalry, castles, and local levies need different supplies. A stronger wall is useful only with people and stores. Defense against Mongol cavalry cannot depend solely on one decisive battle. Warning, moving livestock, and an organized contraction can preserve the population and trained forces needed for a later recovery.

[Diplomacy] Relations with Poland, Hungary, Lithuania, and the khan involve separate questions of marriage, borders, tribute, and passage. Appeals against Mongol power do not guarantee joint intervention. Commands from Mongol envoys require local implementation, forcing princes to weigh their cost against the risks of refusal.

[Costs and fallback] Boyars have resisted princely consolidation, while towns and villages cannot build and campaign without limit. Conditional confirmation of rights, shared garrison costs, and family cooperation reduce internal losses. If plans fail, preserve people, craftsmen, and Volhynian supply routes. The crown and foreign connections remain instruments for recovery rather than reasons to continue an unaffordable war.
genoa:
[Harbor and overseas stations] Liguria's steep hinterland makes seaborne food important to Genoa, linking the city's everyday welfare to warehouses, repairs, and safe arrivals. Aleria and Pantikapaion lie far apart and require separate arrangements for access and supply. A large fleet on one route cannot simultaneously protect every merchant station. Ships in port also need timber, rigging, crews, and credit before they can sail. Policy must distinguish commercial contact, negotiated privilege, and direct territorial possession; each provides a different kind of resource and imposes a different obligation on the commune.

[Captaincy and powerful families] Guglielmo Boccanegra has held the popular captaincy since 1257, governing through councils and a network of supporters. Doria, Spinola, Grimaldi, and other families possess different commercial and political connections. Popular authority does not imply that every urban group directly makes the same decisions, nor does a family name establish an unchanging foreign alignment. The captain must provide enough order for exchange while preventing private quarrels from capturing communal resources. Access to office, courts, and rewards for service therefore matters alongside the formal title of the government.

[Credit and naval expense] Commercial profits belong to families and partnerships; the commune obtains agreed dues, loans, and services rather than the full value of every cargo. A fleet requires cash, equipment, and crews removed from other employment. Creditors need a plausible means of repayment and confidence in the courts. A government that confiscates repeatedly may fund one operation while losing access to the next loan. Predictable treatment of merchants and a clear division of public and private obligations support both military endurance and the food supply of the city.

[Fleets and coastal defense] Galleys, transports, and coastal defenders perform different tasks. Crews, water, sailing seasons, and repairs limit long-distance operations, and a naval victory can leave expensive convoy obligations behind it. Protecting grain ships may be more urgent than pursuing an enemy squadron. The commune needs a concentration it can supply, together with instructions about prizes and private property. Otherwise a campaign presented as communal defense can become a source of quarrels among those who furnished vessels, lent money, or expected compensation for losses.

[Saint Sabas and diplomatic choices] The setback at Acre in 1258 has damaged Genoese access and commercial position without ending every possibility of exchange. Venice, Pisa, Latin lordships, and Nicaea have different interests in customs, quarters, and shipping. Religious affiliation or the language of Guelf and Ghibelline cannot alone determine a workable agreement. A proposed privilege is valuable only if the partner can enforce it and Genoese merchants can reach it. Embassies must therefore assess protection and local jurisdiction as carefully as an offer of favorable charges.

[Sharing losses and retaining a fallback] Great families, shipowners, artisans, and borrowers bear different risks. The government needs a credible division of military costs, compensation, and gains from privileges. A limited truce, shorter convoy commitments, or reciprocal trade can preserve strength without settling every rivalry. If a blockade and naval defeat coincide, food for the home port and confidence in communal repayment take priority over prestige at a distant station. An overseas venture should have a defined obligation and a means of withdrawal, so a failed bargain does not consume the city that financed it.
georgia:
[Geography] Kutaisi and Tbilisi link western valleys, eastern uplands, and Armenian routes; Yerevan and Baghaberd extend the supply and defense problem. Mountains delay armies but also slow revenue, relief, and food transport. They do not make the country naturally unconquerable. Control of passes and the willingness of local holders determine how a position can actually be defended.

[Legitimacy] David VI and David VII share a kingship shaped by Mongol recognition, dynastic descent, and ecclesiastical tradition. Western and eastern lords have different expectations of service, taxation, and the power of the two kings, making continued cooperation essential.

[Revenue] Estates, vines and grain, local exchange, and city dues provide resources, while Mongol taxation, embassies, and military service draw on the same surplus. Church property and noble rights limit central collection. Goods crossing the Caucasus do not all become royal income; transport, protection, and local retention must be paid first.

[Forces] Noble cavalry, royal followers, and castle troops can defend passes but have also served in Mongol campaigns. Operations at Alamut in 1256 and Baghdad in 1258 form background without implying an unlimited reserve. Service abroad can weaken home defense and turn a bargain for protection into deeper dependence on the authority demanding the troops.

[Diplomacy] Mongol commanders, Armenia, Rum, and Byzantine connections provide different channels. A foreign alliance does not settle jurisdiction between royal branches, and one submission does not bind every lord. Rising demands may provoke resistance, while punitive expeditions and internal disputes would both damage production.

[Costs and fallback] Those paying tribute may not be those receiving campaign spoils. The crown must not conceal distributional conflict with repeated taxation. Defined service periods, church protection, and local guarantees can reduce pressure. After a setback, retain connected valleys, move livestock, and negotiate reduced service or a truce while preserving the people needed to restore production.
granada:
[River ports and mountain connections] Nasrid government presently relies on Seville and Guejar Castle, positions with different defensive and provisioning needs. Seville's quays, stores, and agricultural approaches require protection; Guejar depends more directly on guarded routes through difficult terrain. Seville connects the Guadalquivir to Atlantic exchange through cultivation, quays, and river approaches, while Guejar offers a different defensive setting. Connections with southern mountain communities, coastal exchange, and irrigated Andalusian society give the dynasty several sources of cooperation. Actual command nevertheless requires defenders, written obligations, and people willing to honor them. River carriage still requires loading, protection, and suitable conditions; the presence of a port does not guarantee unlimited grain for an army.

[The bargaining foundations of a dynasty] Muhammad I rose at Arjona in 1232 amid the disintegration of Almohad authority and competition with Ibn Hud. In 1246 he surrendered Jaén, accepted Ferdinand III's overlordship, and secured a twenty-year truce; he later renewed allegiance to Alfonso X. This arrangement links submission and payment to continued rule elsewhere. It neither gives Castile direct appointment of every official nor abolishes Nasrid religious identity. Muhammad's assistance to Castile at Seville in 1248 demonstrates actual political cooperation across confessional boundaries. Present control of Seville again gives the two courts direct interests in southern rights; previous cooperation does not settle every current dispute. Legitimacy still requires balancing commitments abroad with the expectations of Muslim inhabitants and the dynasty's ability to protect them.

[Irrigation, exchange, and competing demands] Nasrid agriculture and exchange include silk and dried fruit. Incoming displaced people bring skills and labor alongside settlement costs. Irrigation requires maintenance, allocation of water, and resolution of land disputes; it is not a costless natural treasury. Work on the Alhambra's defensive and residential complex has begun, but continued construction requires stone, skilled labor, water, and transport. Building, defense, and tribute to Castile compete for resources. An official collecting the current payment without regard to seed and livestock can undermine the next season's production. Effective returns depend on collectors, local partners, and continued access to markets. Possession of a city does not make every market, property, and religious endowment available for unlimited extraction without negotiation.

[Fortresses, cavalry, and concentrated population] Placing trusted men in towns and castles links defense to dynastic confidence, while also increasing dependence on relatives and local partners. Mounted forces can scout, raid, and screen a frontier, but garrisons and infantry perform different tasks. Mountain roads, confined approaches, and river positions offer protection while constraining a sortie's retreat. Displaced people entering towns increase manpower and skills but also food, water, and sanitary pressures during siege. Maintaining skilled mounted troops is costly, and trained men and good horses cannot be replaced as quickly as a temporary levy. Prolonged war intensifies competition between maintaining mounts, repairing walls, and working fields. A stronger fortress does not eliminate the value of a negotiated truce or guarantee that every district can be defended simultaneously.

[Tributary peace and the Maghreb] Peace with Castile offers time for internal consolidation, while the treatment of Muslim communities across the border still shapes confidence. Muhammad renewed his obligations at Alfonso's court in 1254. Tribute buys breathing space while creating a burden capable of attracting criticism. North African connections provide diplomatic and economic possibilities, but Marinids, Almohads, Zayyanids, and Hafsids have separate conflicts. Shared religion does not make each an instantly available military reserve. Northwestern approaches and coastal access can be more vulnerable than the highest ridges, while commercial safety requires arrangements across political boundaries. Seville's river routes and competing claims make northern pressure more than a matter of mountain barriers; payments and military commitments must remain compatible with productive land and commercial access.

[Families, cooperation, and survival costs] Relatives and allies participate in local government; the Banu Ashqilula are part of Muhammad's political network. Their local resources make cooperation valuable while also raising the risks of concentrated office and revenue. The court needs dependable commanders without allowing particular families to monopolize jurisdiction and income. Scholars, merchants, soldiers, and cultivators may evaluate accommodation with Castile differently: religious standing matters, but so do an open market and protection from raiding. Refusal of every concession may preserve a slogan while destroying the means of protecting subjects. Unrestrained collection to satisfy tribute can equally wear away domestic acceptance. Renewed truces, revised payments, and limited concessions provide alternatives for preserving the core. Survival is not a predestined outcome but the result of choices that remain materially and politically affordable.
hafsid:
[Coasts and oasis communications] Hafsid possessions extend from Tunis and Sfax to Béjaïa, Constantine, Algiers, Biskra, Ouargla, and other inland positions. Maritime towns connect Mediterranean carriage with roads carrying grain, animals, and desert trade. Shipping has advantages over land transport but still depends on season, harbor access, and protection. Caravans require water, pack animals, guides, and agreements along the route; a royal command cannot produce an uninterrupted stream of gold. Distances and local influence shape collection and relief. Acknowledgment of one ruler does not erase local collection, retained rights, and transport obligations; not every receipt immediately reaches Tunis. Protecting agricultural and pastoral production is as necessary to urban provisioning and defense as access to lucrative foreign goods.

[From provincial authority to caliphal claims] The Hafsid family has ties to the Almohad movement and its elite, but Abu Zakariya's independent rule established a separate center in Ifriqiya. Muhammad al-Mustansir succeeded in 1249 and claimed caliphal status in 1253. Baghdad's fall in 1258 intensifies questions of Islamic authority and recognition. A title supplies prestige without automatically creating effective command over rival dynasties; recognition from different communities carries different expectations. Emir, sultan, and caliph also convey different claims rather than interchangeable offices. Cooperation in Tunis, Béjaïa, and among rural leaders still depends on governing relationships. The state inherits earlier experience while building its own dynastic order, rather than remaining an ordinary province waiting for instructions from Marrakech. Claimed universal standing and the territory it can actually administer are different resources.

[Commerce, cultivation, and expenditure] Port exchange, markets, agricultural dues, and inland traffic provide varied income shaped by treaties, local rights, and collection. Diplomatic gifts, religious standing, the household, and military obligations all compete for resources. An occasional gift or embassy does not provide the recurring receipts needed to maintain the court and its defenders. Desert exchange involves numerous powers: Hafsid authorities may benefit at controlled nodes without claiming all profits from distant gold-producing regions. Andalusian newcomers enlarge commercial, artisanal, and intellectual resources while requiring accommodation, property, and protection. Local custom, promises of protection, and specific privileges constrain collection, while officials must balance receipts against retaining commerce. Foreign privileges define particular duties and protections, limiting arbitrary demands while preserving negotiated receipts. Durable income requires credible terms and continued traffic.

[Urban defense and tribal mobilization] The dynasty needs dependable household forces and cooperation with chiefs and provincial interests. Duties, rewards, and geographical reach need not be identical among contingents. Mounted troops can patrol or interrupt routes, while walled towns require infantry, grain, and repairs. Merchant shipping does not constitute an unlimited permanent navy; long-distance carriage needs crews, water, and payment. Excessive western campaigning or rural requisition can deprive Tunis and other centers while encouraging resistance. Oasis security calls for defended points, escorts, and negotiation rather than imagining an army pursuing opponents indefinitely through waterless terrain. Chiefs' contributions depend on rewards, pasture, and needs at home. Service terms and provisions must be settled before separate contingents can sustain a common campaign.

[Commercial agreements and competing claims] Italian and Aragonese merchants offer both cooperation and competition. Religious difference does not prevent agreements, and trading connections do not guarantee friendship. The neighboring Zayyanids pursue survival on their own terms, while the Marinids expand farther west. Restoring every former Almohad possession is not a sufficient explanation of all Hafsid policy. Egyptian and Syrian crises affect Mediterranean power and religious standing without placing those armies under Tunisian command. Maritime conflict threatens customs and grain carriage. The court must watch unfamiliar fleets while keeping existing agreements credible. Port access, compensation, escorts, and diplomatic complaints can be negotiated separately rather than turning one dispute into hostility toward all foreign merchants. Maintaining access, dividing hostile combinations, and preserving options for commerce and pilgrimage are attainable objectives.

[The center's bargains with local interests] Urban notables value exchange and jurisdiction, chiefs value mobilization terms and rewards, and scholars defend institutions and authority. They may support the dynasty without sharing every project. Expanding royal titles increases expectations of patronage, building, and protection. Revenue granted to supporters limits central resources, but abrupt increases in demands can also encourage evasion and withdrawal. Tunis and western cities have their own notables and provisioning networks. Officials monopolizing rewards and collection may weaken common authority, making communication and fair adjudication as important as foreign prestige. If a frontier campaign fails, preserving Tunis, principal food routes, commercial agreements, and localized truces offers a recovery position. Prestige becomes durable obedience only when linked to obligations communities can continue to bear.
holy:
[Regions and communications] The Rhine, Danube, Saxon lands, and northern trading towns form connected networks under different local authorities. Aachen, Cologne, Frankfurt, Vienna, and the other holdings need distinct supplies and agreements. Distance matters even where a court claims the same overarching jurisdiction. River crossings and roads can connect resources, but the holders of tolls, bridges, and fortresses decide how readily they move. An imperial campaign therefore requires a negotiated chain of cooperation rather than an assumption that every region functions as a royal estate.

[Disputed kingship] The struggles following the deaths of Frederick II and Conrad IV have prevented generally accepted central leadership. In 1257 Richard of Cornwall and Alfonso of Castile received competing electoral support. Election as king of the Romans, imperial coronation, and practical obedience are different matters. A prince may acknowledge a title while limiting military or financial obligations. The court must turn recognition into stated assistance, and it must consider what confirmation costs when another lord claims the same right or expects an equivalent reward.

[Revenues and privileges] Royal property, relations with towns, passage rights, and minting can yield income, but pledges and local privileges limit what is disposable. Princes do not deliver all receipts to a central treasury. Towns bargain for protection and jurisdiction rather than promise unlimited service. Restraining feuds and repeated charges may improve traffic while reducing the gains of particular holders. A ruler needs a credible settlement of those losses, since a reform announced without regional support may merely encourage a new toll or an armed challenge on another stretch of river.

[Service and military agreements] Princely followings, city contingents, and paid retainers serve for different terms and purposes. An imperial claim does not assemble every knight automatically. Sieges, mountain crossings, and an Italian journey demand funds and provisions beyond the first gathering. Agreements should specify garrisons, transport, duration, and withdrawal. A smaller contingent with clear duties can provide more useful security than a larger nominal host whose leaders expect incompatible rewards or return home as soon as their customary obligation ends.

[Papacy and neighboring powers] The papacy, France, England, Castile, Bohemia, and Italian cities influence recognition and resources in different ways. Kinship may provide money while drawing a king into another realm's quarrels. Mediation and confirmation can produce immediate gains where a general restoration of earlier imperial power would provoke resistance. North and south of the Alps require separate bargains.
