A papal agreement cannot alone secure every city, just as electoral support cannot oblige a distant lord to finance an expedition that threatens his own position.

[Local costs and fallback] Concessions can buy support, but excessive grants leave fewer resources for the next mobilization. Reclaiming old rights can instead create a hostile coalition. Retain dependable towns, routes, and princely relationships, and use regional peace to build credit. If necessary, defer coronation and tolerate unresolved claims while preserving a capacity to act. Imperial dignity is useful when it helps settle a dispute or secure cooperation; it becomes a liability when interpreted as a promise to win every conflict immediately, regardless of the resources supporters will provide.
hungary:
[Rivers and frontier mountains] The Danube and Tisza carry food but also separate garrisons whose relief depends on crossings. Western towns, open pasture, and Transylvanian passes require different defense. Ferries, fodder, mining roads, and winter stores determine response time. A fortified point is useful when it protects a route and can be supplied, not merely because its walls appear formidable. The crown must decide which corridors connect its agricultural and urban resources and which isolated positions would consume more aid than they could protect.

[Kingship and reconstruction] Béla IV has ruled since 1235, and the invasion of 1241–1242 damaged population, revenue, and defense. Recovery requires adjusting earlier efforts to reclaim land alongside new opportunities for nobles and settlers. The tradition of Saint Stephen's crown sustains legitimacy without removing the bargaining power of nobles, churches, and royal branches. A grant can encourage rebuilding and reward service while reducing direct royal income. The king must obtain an identifiable return rather than regard every new castle or privileged settlement as an unconditional extension of central authority.

[Revenue and population] Agriculture, salt, minerals, markets, and royal estates yield different resources. Recovery needs inhabitants, skills, and dependable rules. Town privileges and church exemptions limit collection, while ore becomes usable money only after extraction and transport. A levy that interrupts cultivation can deprive a castle of its future supplies. The government should distinguish a district's potential from receipts actually available for wages, and preserve reserves for poor harvests and threats beyond the frontier receiving most attention at court.

[Castles and mounted forces] Stone fortresses, noble followings, royal troops, and mobile Cuman cavalry complement one another, with different requirements for water, grain, horses, and service. A field battle on the plain is not the same task as defending a pass. Conflict between Cuman grazing and cultivation can turn a useful military resource into a domestic crisis. Clear obligations and protection for affected communities make cooperation more durable than alternating between unrestricted demands on mounted allies and hostility toward their presence.

[Styria and neighboring interests] Arrangements in Styria since 1254 remain contested by Bohemia, local lords, and Hungarian interests. Relationships in the Balkans and the steppe direction also require a reserve. Marriage, confirmation of estates, and ecclesiastical mediation can reduce the need to campaign everywhere. Local supporters of a claim must be assessed for the assistance they can deliver, since a title without accepted officials or supplies may impose an expensive obligation rather than add revenue to the crown.

[Distribution and fallback] A noble's castle, a town's privilege, and a pastoral group's grazing rights can each reduce another constituency's gains. Predictable military, judicial, and financial duties help the monarchy hold these interests together. After a setback, accept a limited frontier compromise while preserving recovered communities and a connected chain of defenses. Western prestige is not worth consuming every reserve needed for another invasion. Keeping a paid guard and supporters willing to return can provide more lasting strength than an enlarged claim whose enforcement the realm cannot afford.
ilkhanate:
[Mesopotamia and Iranian communications] Baghdad, Mosul, and Tabriz link rivers, passes, and upland pasture, with different requirements for supply. Azerbaijan and Anatolian roads provide western approaches, but winter, water levels, and the needs of horse herds constrain mobility. A rapid advance can outrun secure collection and leave officials dependent on local protection. The government must maintain usable crossings and intermediate stores as well as the fighting column, since a town's submission does not guarantee that animals, grain, or transport will be ready whenever a commander demands them.

[Commission and family authority] As Möngke's brother and the commander entrusted with western operations, Hulagu relies on the service of noyans and their followings. Alamut's capture in 1256 and Baghdad's fall in 1258 have transformed regional authority without causing every Mongol prince to relinquish a claim to shares or influence. Command and court access still require allocation. The great khan's authorization provides standing, while local compliance depends on decisions about officials, revenue, religion, and the protection of communities from unauthorized exactions by different military parties.

[Assessment and recovery] Iranian officials, towns, and cultivation can sustain enduring rule, but war damage, repeated demands, and the use of cultivated land for grazing weaken receipts. Gifts, tribute, and plunder often provide one-time resources. Continuing revenue needs inhabitants, irrigation, and assessments that can actually be met. Commanders competing for the same surplus may obtain less in total while provoking flight. Distinguishing what belongs to military support, the ruler's treasury, and recognized local rights helps convert conquest into a district that can repeatedly supply the government.

[Mounted warfare and sieges] Mongol mobility depends on spare horses, pasture, and coordination, while sieges need craftsmen, equipment, and transport. Allied contingents add people and knowledge of terrain but carry costs for their own districts. A campaign on several fronts requires clear service and supply arrangements. Earlier victories do not remove the need to assess water, fodder, and the time required to replace losses. Keeping a reserve and a supported line of withdrawal can protect the value of a successful advance better than committing every available contingent to an uncertain pursuit.

[Syria and the Caucasus] Syrian towns, Egypt, Armenia, Georgia, and Rum separately weigh protection and submission. Berke also has interests in Caucasian routes, pasture, and revenue. One ruler's agreement establishes a particular arrangement rather than lasting obedience from every ally or resident. Envoys can clarify service, preserve trade, and reduce the danger of simultaneous disputes. The ruler should distinguish an opponent who might accept terms from a town unable to perform them, since treating both as identical enemies may destroy resources while adding avoidable commitments.

[Domestic costs and fallback] Commanders seek rewards, officials need collectable assessments, towns need security, and pastoral followers need grass. Satisfying one can reduce another's gains. Installments, confirmation of local rights, and restrictions on unauthorized plunder help preserve production. If western operations fail, save the troops and horses, contract to positions that can support them, and negotiate limited tribute or a truce. Consolidating what can be held is a practical means of preserving authority; an additional devastated district may provide neither income nor a defensible frontier.
kiev:
[River and hinterland] The Dnieper connects Kyiv with northern Rus and the southern steppe, but usable passage requires boats, shore roads, and protection along the route. Bila Cerkva, Korsun, Vinnytsia, and Kaniv have resources of their own that cannot all reach the capital on command. Floods, ice, and raiding change the conditions of movement. The ruler must identify stores, crossings, and places of refuge before an emergency, since the apparent continuity of a river on a map conceals the separate authorities and transport arrangements needed to use it.

[An old capital and recognition] The capture of 1240 damaged defenses and population without extinguishing ecclesiastical institutions or princely traditions. Kyiv's former standing attracts claims from several families, while the khan and northeastern Rus influence recognition. A ruler must make a title meaningful locally through protection and justice. Older authority over other Rus lands does not establish their present obedience or deliver their receipts. The useful question is which communities and neighboring holders will cooperate, on what terms, and whether the government can honor the guarantees it offers.

[Restoring revenue] Estates, markets, crafts, and river traffic can restore receipts if residents remain and fields can be harvested. Church property and local retention limit the princely share, while tribute consumes surplus. Restraining repeated exactions and protecting travelers can rebuild confidence more effectively than an assessment based on the city's earlier prosperity. Food, seed, labor, and transport must be distinguished from disposable money. A demand that removes the seed or animals needed for the next season may satisfy an official once while leaving the district less able to support either a garrison or another payment.

[Defense and warning] Retainers, local warriors, and town guards need to protect crossings, stores, and routes of refuge. They should not be committed to an unrestricted pursuit of cavalry across the plain. Earth-and-timber works and repaired masonry both require people and supplies. Holding a famous city without relief can magnify losses. Warning from neighboring towns and dispersed stores may preserve more strength than concentrating every resource behind one wall. Defensive service also needs a defined duration so households can continue the cultivation that sustains the next mobilization.

[The khan and neighboring lands] The khan, Chernigov, Galicia, and northeastern Rus pursue different interests. Passage, tribute, investiture, and recognition among relatives require separate negotiation; submission on one issue does not settle every right. Southern routes offer commercial opportunities but can also bring an army rapidly toward the city. Envoys need reliable information about who can enforce a promise. An agreement with a distant court may still require a local holder to protect a crossing or restrain demands on merchants and cultivators.

[Domestic costs and fallback] Churches, towns, and villages need a share of a limited surplus. Appointments and collection that benefit only relatives can drive residents away. Defined assessments and credible justice, together with truces that allow cultivation, help rebuild a local base. After a setback, preserve inhabitants, craftsmen, records, and northern access. The city's prestige can assist renewed bargaining when it is supported by people and resources; it cannot substitute for them. A restricted but functioning government retains more room for recovery than an impressive title attached to an abandoned district.
latinempire:
[Capital and dispersed positions] Constantinople, Adrianople, Thessalonica, and positions toward Trebizond and Sinope extend the problem across land and sea. The straits have great value, but walls still require imported grain and available vessels. A distant station may offer contact or impose a convoy obligation. The emperor needs distinct arrangements for each route rather than assume one imperial claim creates a continuous supply system. Markets, warehouses, and local cooperation determine whether a port can contribute to the capital or must first receive assistance itself.

[Imperial title and local recognition] The arrangements following the Fourth Crusade left an imperial crown alongside particular Venetian and aristocratic rights. Greek residents and ecclesiastical institutions retain relationships of their own. Baldwin II's dynastic standing does not remove bargaining by partners, and claims to the earlier empire do not create collectable income. The court must specify what service, protection, or jurisdiction follows from recognition. A concession that secures a fleet may reduce future receipts, while a demand to revoke privileges may deprive the capital of the very ships on which its defense depends.

[Scarce money and credit] Estates, customs, and assistance are constrained by war and privileges. Relics, pledges, and western family connections may produce immediate money while reducing later options. Repeatedly promising the same receipts damages credit. Grain prices, guards, and repairs have immediate claims on the treasury. The court must distinguish a promised grant from money received, and a merchant's private profit from public revenue. Clear repayment and protection terms can preserve a source of credit that confiscation would close, making restraint a practical part of defending the capital.

[Walls, troops, and ships] Latin lords, paid soldiers, residents, and maritime partners provide different services. Walls resist an attack but cannot replace food, wages, or observation at sea. Losing a field force can make defense of the city harder even if the fortifications remain intact. Terms of service and naval commitments need confirmation before an expedition begins. A defensible plan combines stocked positions with a reserve and a route for relief, rather than treating the reputation of Constantinople's walls as a sufficient answer to every military threat.

[Nicaea and western partners] Nicaea seeks Roman imperial authority, while Bulgaria, Venice, and western princes pursue independent objectives. A religious appeal can attract attention without guaranteeing timely relief. Diplomacy should first obtain grain access, navigation, and a buffer before seeking a general reconquest. Partners need a defined return that the court can honor. An extravagant promise of land or revenue can create another dispute if local holders refuse it, and a patron asked for unlimited assistance may decide that neutrality or a different commercial arrangement is more useful.

[Residents and a fallback] Greek and Latin communities, clergy, lords, and merchants do not acquire identical interests simply because they face a common danger. Property protection, credible justice, and food reduce the cost of internal disagreement. If pressure grows, maritime supply, limited privileges, and a guaranteed truce may preserve ports that can be supported. The government needs residents and credit as well as an imperial title. Retaining a functioning harbor and willing partners gives it choices that an overextended collection of unprovisioned claims cannot provide.
lithuania:
[Forests and river corridors] The Nemunas, Baltic forests, and Black Ruthenian approaches form distinct political zones. Kernavė, Novogrudok, Grodno, and northern strongholds are not a territory without intervening rights and interests. Passage requires local cooperation; marshes and winter can change routes. A holding is useful when it connects supporters and supplies, not simply when it extends a claim on a map. River crossings also concentrate risk: they offer trade and communications while exposing travelers to those who hold the banks, boats, and adjoining roads.

[Crown and local oaths] Mindaugas accepted baptism in 1251 and a crown in 1253, establishing relationships with the papacy and the Livonian Order. This strengthens his standing without eliminating family competition or pagan practice. Promises concerning land and actual obedience from its inhabitants are separate political matters. The king needs followers who gain from his rule and neighbors who can enforce an agreement. Religious recognition may reduce one source of pressure while making a concession harder to explain to leaders whose land, ritual, or authority is affected.

[Resources and service] Tribute, cultivation, animals, markets, and spoils supply the king and local leaders. Raiding does not yield a stable annual assessment. A prolonged assembly removes labor from fields and herds, while distant positions require guards, gifts, and repeated negotiation. Safe exchange can provide a more dependable gain than continual plunder. The ruler must divide rewards without promising all future receipts to immediate supporters, and preserve enough food and animals for communities to answer another summons rather than disperse after the first expedition.

[Forces and terrain] Mounted followings, local infantry, and garrisons perform different tasks. Skill in forest raiding does not establish the ability to take every fortified position. Scouting, withdrawal routes, distribution of spoils, and service periods influence cooperation. Against the orders, a long siege can consume advantages in local movement by creating fixed supply needs. Commanders should identify a limited purpose for a gathering and retain a route home, rather than interpret every temporary military success as the beginning of an unlimited campaign.

[Orders and Rus neighbors] Livonian and Prussian interests and the neighboring Rus lands are not a single enemy. The crown may seek peace in the west while strengthening influence southward. Samogitian leaders also act independently, so court support must be judged by the cooperation it can actually secure. Promising land beyond dependable control can create claims without producing obedience. Marriages, protected passage, and recognition of a relative's position can sometimes achieve a durable connection with fewer costs than maintaining an army in a hostile district.

[Religious costs and fallback] External recognition, local ritual, and family interests may conflict. Forcing immediate uniformity can narrow the coalition supporting the king. Defined obligations and local guarantees can maintain cooperation while disagreements remain. After a setback, retain core routes, negotiate truces separately, and preserve people, horses, and family support. These provide a basis for deciding whether a distant claim can be renewed. A wider nominal kingship that alienates the communities expected to defend it may leave the crown weaker than a limited agreement with obligations its followers accept.
mamluk:
[Nile and northern connections] Cairo, Fayyum, Upper Egypt, and Alexandria depend on river transport and the agricultural cycle, while Syrian and Hijazi routes require desert supplies. Damascus, Aleppo, and northern positions have local people and receipts of their own; Egypt cannot send unlimited food to each. Boats, wells, pack animals, and guarded stages convert distance into an operational cost. The government must distinguish protection of the Nile core from support for a frontier, since both use resources that remain essential to maintaining the court and the military households.

[Government and military households] The changes of 1250 and Aybak's death in 1257 have left competition among military households. Formal succession still needs acceptance from commanders. Military achievement, protection of religious institutions, and allocation of income together support authority. Appointment and command that benefit only one group can create opposition among others whose troops the ruler needs. The practical aim is an agreement that can mobilize forces while leaving enough confidence for cooperation after the immediate danger, rather than an impressive title unsupported by the officers controlling armed followings.

[Agriculture, ports, and equipment] Agricultural collection and allocated military income sustain mounted forces. Alexandria and Red Sea exchange provide money and goods, while irrigation, transport, and local government also consume receipts. Not every commercial profit belongs to the sultan. Extraordinary military costs cannot be shifted indefinitely to cultivators without reducing the next harvest and assessment. Horses, equipment, and trained men require continuing expenditure. Protecting production and dependable routes is therefore part of military preparation, not a civilian concern that can simply wait until all external threats have disappeared.

[Mounted forces and supply] Training, archery, coordinated command, and reconnaissance matter, but horses, arrows, water, and food determine endurance. Households need agreements over leadership and gains. The same forces cannot remain in every town while campaigning in the field. Desert movement particularly requires stores and protected access to wells. A plan should identify the route, reserves, and conditions for withdrawal before the army commits itself, avoiding a pursuit that leaves its supply exposed or a garrison promise that consumes the force needed for the main threat.

[Mongol pressure and regional partners] Baghdad's fall changes assessments of danger, while Syrian rulers, Latin polities, and Hulagu's followers maintain different relationships. Envoys can clarify intentions and seek passage or bounded neutrality. Religion or military background does not automatically make every neighboring government an ally. A promise to defend every frontier without retreat may be less useful than a credible arrangement to preserve the core and a force capable of intervention. Agreements should be assessed against available ships, food, and troops rather than declarations alone.

[Domestic cost and fallback] Officers seek income, towns need security, religious scholars consider lawful collection, and cultivators sustain production. Emergency demands need limits and recognition. After a setback, preserve the military core, horses, and Nile food routes, using a truce or buffer to obtain recovery time. Repeated purges or destruction of a revenue district can remove support when another mobilization is required. Retaining people who can serve and produce again provides more durable strength than taking a town whose stores, inhabitants, and surrounding cultivation have been exhausted.
marinid:
[Fez and the coastal positions] Marinid holdings include Fez, Salé, Tangier, and Amergou Castle, connecting an inland center, coastal gateways, and local defenses. Fez is already a political and economic base, not an enemy capital awaiting capture. Coastal access still requires food, crews, storage, and safe roads. Zanata mobility and pastoral backgrounds explain some followings without reducing the entire state to tents and raiding. Urban hinterlands, crafts, markets, and traveling merchants provide different resources. An army continually damaging nearby production may reduce the income won through expansion. Almohad and Tlemcen factions retain their own positions across the region, and the coast is not an uncontested corridor along which forces can move without cost.

[Recognition of an emerging government] The Marinid family expanded as Almohad authority weakened and tribal and provincial interests broke away. This differs from the preceding dynasty's foundation through a comprehensive religious reform movement. Abu Yusuf Yaqub succeeded Abu Yahya in 1258, making consolidation of succession and local obedience immediate concerns. The court must turn allegiance won in war into enduring local obligations. Military achievement, family connections, urban protection, and religious patronage can all win recognition, but each comes with expectations. Scholars, judges, and religious institutions can win urban trust for a new ruler, but defend their own property and traditions. Patronage requires continued support beyond promises made during a campaign. Moving beyond a victorious following requires maintaining markets, courts, and worship as well as rewarding soldiers.

[Revenues beyond booty] Towns, cultivation, and passage provide recurring income, while captured property is episodic. Grants of land or revenue strengthen supporters but reduce direct royal access; unchecked successive demands can drive merchants away and cultivators into avoidance. Rights to collect, local receipts, and remittances reaching the court are different resources, further divided by grants to supporters. Military spending must follow disposable funds, not the full value of goods passing through markets. Resources must therefore be judged against controlled positions and effective collection. Protecting commerce does not entitle the ruler to unlimited merchant credit, and an active harbor does not guarantee that enough war transports can be hired at any moment. Managing nearby fields, irrigation water, and regularly supplied urban markets turns conquest into supportable government rather than a cycle requiring another campaign to pay the previous one.

[Tribal mobilization and operations] Forces depend on loyal tribes, associated groups, and potentially other recruits. Leaders who provide men and mounts retain bargaining power. Cavalry can scout, move rapidly, and interrupt roads, while sieges demand infantry, equipment, provisions, and time. The transfer of former Almohad soldiers into new service illustrates that payment and circumstances can redirect allegiance; ethnicity does not predetermine permanent loyalty. Mustering requires communication and preparation; pastures, the condition of mounts, and carried provisions constrain both numbers and the duration of service. Keeping the main mounted force before one city reduces protection elsewhere. Campaigning beyond the straits adds the need for transport and receiving allies. Courage alone does not substitute for any of these conditions.

[Marrakech, eastern neighbors, and the straits] The Almohads retain a dynastic core at Marrakech and are competitors rather than vanished relics. Zayyanids and Hafsids have their own diplomatic options and need not accept leadership from Fez because of shared religion. Granada may seek room under Castilian pressure, but involvement there cannot erase domestic commitments. Crossing the straits first requires agreement over vessels, receiving allies, and shared costs. Christian maritime capabilities deserve assessment, and ports such as Salé need watchmen, crews, stores, and gate defenders able to cooperate promptly. Trade arrangements, presents, truces, and agreements with particular chiefs can divide hostile combinations. Avoiding simultaneous counterattack may produce more durable gains than attaching maximal demands to every neighboring dispute.

[Distribution and the costs of integration] Royal relatives, tribal leaders, urban notables, and religious authorities can support the same government while expecting different offices, resources, safety, and protections. Unequal distribution or a missed payment can weaken military allegiance; towns repeatedly treated as booty may prefer a more predictable arrangement. Rewards must be balanced against resources retained for government. External campaigns cannot permanently conceal these conflicts. If operations against Marrakech stall, consolidating Fez and the ports, securing travel, and accepting a limited truce provide a practical retreat. That is not surrender of ambition but recognition that institutions and revenues require time to stabilize. Production and local credit can prevent one reverse from becoming a general departure of allies. Further expansion requires renewed bargains, reliable provisioning, and defenders who can remain in service without exhausting their own communities.
milan:
[City and plain] Milan's cultivated plain, water management, and grain markets support a concentrated population. Routes toward the Alps connect northern travelers, while approaches to the Adda influence relations with neighboring towns. The city is the principal holding, and an ally at a distance is not a secure agricultural hinterland. Food prices, roads, and storage shape the ability to assemble and maintain troops. Civic government must protect access to produce without assuming every supplier shares Milan's political objectives or will continue trading when transport becomes dangerous.

[Commune and family power] Martino della Torre's authority draws on the popular party and civic offices, while great families, guilds, and deliberative institutions continue to influence legitimacy. Family lordship does not simply abolish communal forms. Excluding established nobles can concentrate support but may also send opponents in search of outside assistance. Offices, courts, and the disposition of confiscated property become means of holding a coalition together. A government that claims to represent the city must demonstrate how ordinary exchange and protection benefit from the concentration of power.

[Manufacture and credit] Crafts, markets, transit, and property provide resources, but private profit is not a tax paid in full to the ruler. Guilds, churches, and families hold particular rights. Loans depend on credible courts and receipts that can repay them. Unclear contributions can discourage lending, and extraordinary requisitions can interrupt food supply. Clear accounts and a defined return for service make it easier to obtain money again. Repeatedly treating wealthy opponents as a substitute treasury instead makes every change of faction threaten the security of commerce.

[Civic and paid forces] Knights, civic contingents, and paid troops have different equipment, service periods, and expectations of reward. A gathering is not a permanent army. Wall defense, protection of roads, and a siege against a neighboring town compete for money. A prolonged operation also removes artisans from employment and unsettles markets at home. Commanders need defined objectives and a plan for replacement and withdrawal, since an apparent military opportunity may become a greater threat to civic cooperation than the opponent it was intended to defeat.

[Lombard relationships] Pallavicino, Ezzelino's interests, neighboring communes, and the papacy pursue different objectives. Factional names alone cannot establish permanent friendship or hostility. The Adda approaches and trading roads can supply common interests even amid political competition. Marriage, truces, and reciprocal recognition can reduce isolation, but promises must fit the troops and food the city can provide. A partner's claim to another town is not automatically a Milanese obligation, especially when intervention would expose the city's own approaches or strengthen a prospective rival.

[Domestic bargains and fallback] The popular coalition includes people with different property and occupations. Food prices, justice, and service obligations matter to them alongside the success of the ruling family. Limited restoration of property, guarantees over office, and an end to private violence can buy room for recovery. After a setback, retain Milan's defenses, food routes, and credit and relinquish advantages that cannot be maintained. Continuing to confiscate in order to sustain an expedition may widen opposition and deprive the government of the cooperation that makes any military force affordable.
mongolian:
[Steppe and distant towns] Volga, Don, and Azov communications connect mobile followings to Black Sea exchange. Basra, Shiraz, Isfahan, and northeastern Iranian holdings have different agricultural and transport conditions. These widely separated nodes cannot function as one continuous pasture. Garrisons and local officials need distinct support, and a commander must know which route can carry food or spare horses. Holding a title over a district does not establish its obedience or make its receipts available at the place where the khan wants to gather an army.

[Jochid shares and authority] Succession after Batu and Berke's position depend on family, aristocratic followings, and relations at the imperial court. Investiture and tribute agreements provide instruments of rule, while local princes retain courts and succession interests. Dependence does not mean every district is managed directly by one office. The khan must balance the rewards expected by his own supporters with the cooperation of rulers who collect and deliver resources. An excessive demand can reduce the capacity of a tributary to provide either the next payment or useful military assistance.

[Tribute and exchange] Rus payments, town receipts, and steppe commerce supply different resources, while animals and horses are also military reserves. Repeated plunder may yield goods once but drive people away and shrink markets. Envoys and intermediaries need limits that prevent several authorities from demanding the same surplus. Dependable assessments and protected passage make repeated payment more likely. The treasury must distinguish a tribute promised by a prince from supplies delivered to a campaign, since transport, local retention, and the requirements of the paying district intervene between them.

[Mounted force and distance] Mounted archery, coordinated columns, and spare horses provide speed, while frozen rivers and pasture determine particular routes. Service from Rus or other dependent forces needs defined duration and supply. Pursuing a distant enemy can wear down horses and expose households and grazing land. Mobility is not unlimited endurance. A plan should keep reserves and a route to supportable ground, identify which contingent carries which duty, and avoid treating every local success as a reason to widen the campaign before the first objective can be held.

[Rus and the Caucasus] Galicia, northeastern Rus, and other princes make different calculations about tribute, investiture, and rivalry with neighbors. The Caucasus involves Hulagu, Armenia, Georgia, and family claims as well as routes and pasture. Marriage, commerce, and service can be negotiated separately. One dispute need not force every partner into a permanent alignment. Reliable reports and intermediaries are essential because a court promise may have little force over a particular crossing or a commander seeking his own share of the gains.

[Distribution and fallback] Nobles, pastoral households, merchants, and dependent princes do not receive the same gains. Rewards that pledge all receipts leave less for the next mobilization. Limited tribute, recognition, and restraint of unauthorized plunder can preserve production. After a setback, concentrate the following that can be supported and retain herds, crossings, and political recognition. These resources allow renewed bargaining and a different allocation of force. An unending pursuit may instead sacrifice the animals, people, and willingness to serve on which the khan's authority depends.
murcia:
[Production along the Segura] Murcia depends on the Segura and its irrigation network, connecting fields, gardens, channels, and urban markets. Lorca Castle and Santa Bárbara Castle also remain under its authority. Defense therefore concerns communication and water as well as one set of walls. Lorca's inland and southern approaches have military value, while coastal connections reach broader exchanges; a trading route does not automatically constitute a customs system monopolized by the emir. Neglected channels and disputed water reduce agricultural dues, raise urban prices, and weaken supplies for defenders. Repeated small-scale destruction of cultivation can be harder to recover from than a battle fought away from the fields. Keeping people working on the land is consequently a strategic resource.

[Hudid inheritance and the protectorate] Following Ibn Hud's death in 1238, Murcia experienced changes of government and increasing outside pressure. In 1243 Prince Alfonso, acting for Ferdinand III, reached the Alcaraz arrangement with Muslim rulers and representatives of leading families. Castilian overlordship, military control, and a share of revenues were exchanged for continued worship, property guarantees, and local government under supervision. Local institutions continue under negotiated protection, while Castile holds superior claims to service and revenue. Acceptance was uneven: Lorca, Mula, and Cartagena resisted and were subsequently conquered. Lorca and the other positions remain under local control, and memories of resistance and intervention sharpen concern over property and final jurisdiction. Local administration and military possession remain distinguishable questions.

[Shared collection and credibility] Part of local income serves the protecting power, while local officials, defense, and irrigation also require resources. The same dues cannot be counted in full by two treasuries. Agriculture, exchange, and community obligations require attention to local practice; different towns and properties may have different obligations requiring clear division between retained income and external payments. Cultivators need confidence in land and water rights to continue producing. Merchants need enforceable contracts and passage without arbitrary seizure more than a title promising protection. Repeated demands by garrisons, lordships, and officials can destroy the bargain's credibility. Clear accounts and identifiable collectors help the local government meet external demands while preserving supplies and the confidence of residents. Maintaining the agreement requires limits as well as payment.

[Fortresses and limited military resources] The Alcaraz arrangements allow for Castilian troops in fortresses alongside local civil government. The local ruler must preserve room for appointment and command within these overlapping relationships. Household followers, urban defenders, and locally mobilized inhabitants are plausible resources drawn from a limited population whose men, equipment, and horses all require sustained support. Prolonged service removes cultivators from channel repair and harvest. A temporarily secure fortress cannot replace productive land outside its walls. Lorca and the other positions can watch approaches, issue warnings, and shelter inhabitants but may become isolated when connecting routes fail. The defensible military objective is protection of people and production rather than continual field operations designed to imitate the strength of a much larger crown.

[Three neighbors and conflicting claims] Castilian demands, the attractions or pressures of Granada, and Aragonese concern over southern expansion constrain local choices. The Almizra settlement of 1244 divides spheres between Aragon and Castile without making Murcian society a territory devoid of its own interests. If earlier guarantees are honored, payment and military supervision may still preserve local institutions. Encroachment on property, worship, or appointments increases the cost of cooperation. Outside rulers may invoke protection, agreements, or kinship to justify intervention. Contradictory promises reduce negotiating space; taxation, garrisons, and jurisdiction need boundaries that both sides can continue to honor.

[Community divisions and usable alternatives] The ruling family, scholars, cultivators, merchants, and leading men of different towns can assess protection differently. Some exchange payment for security; others fear replacement of local authorities. Disagreement over burdens can fragment cooperation even without a common plan of resistance. Fiscal pressure, settlement, and land disputes can shift cooperation, but benefits and burdens are uneven across districts and families, and preferences change with collection and security. Should circumstances deteriorate, revised payments, arbitration, renewed property guarantees, or limited concessions may preserve inhabitants, documents, and local government. Departure is not the only retreat and should not become a plan to destroy the regime's own revenue base. The attainable goal is continued room for cultivation, exchange, and worship among stronger neighbors.
murom:
[Oka and frontier] Murom, Ryazan, Pronsk, Kadom, and Tula connect the Oka woods with the steppe edge. Rivers carry trade and can also guide armies. Roads, ice, and pack transport change the conditions of relief. Woodland does not exclude invasion. The ruler needs warnings from approaches, defensible crossings, and stores that can be moved or protected. A town's survival depends on cooperation with neighboring settlements as well as its own walls, particularly when an attacker can bypass a strong point and threaten the people who supply it.

[Family and succession] Murom, Ryazan, and Pronsk have connected princely traditions and distinct branches. Patrimony and precedence affect recognition. Conquest adds external pressure without removing the needs of churches and towns for protection. A shared title does not settle service among all relatives. Agreements over estates, courts, and military contributions can reduce the chance that a rival seeks backing from a neighbor. The prince must balance inherited claims with possession and local support, since a judgment issued without the means to enforce it may simply reopen the dispute.

[Resources after conquest] Cultivation, livestock, fishing and woodland products, markets, and crossings provide limited resources. Population losses and tribute reduce the disposable balance. Restoring fields requires labor and animals, while construction and service can consume both. Church property and local rights further limit assessment. A ruler should distinguish seed, household food, and productive animals from goods that can safely be collected. Demands that ignore those differences may fund a guard briefly while depriving the district of the resources needed to feed it again.

[Wooden defenses and mounted followers] Retainers, local mounted men, and town guards can protect crossings and provide warning; they cannot sustain an unrestricted race with steppe cavalry. Earth-and-timber works need repairs, water, and food. An isolated post needs instructions for withdrawal rather than an undefined promise of relief. Concentrating a reliable contingent can be more sustainable than keeping every household's workers in camp. Service terms and responsibility for horses and provisions should be agreed before movement, so a defensive gathering does not undermine the cultivation it is meant to protect.

[Khan and neighbors] Tribute, Vladimir's influence, Chernigov family relationships, and other Rus neighbors present different questions. Passage and exchange may continue while a political dispute remains unsettled. Envoys, marriage, and bounded dependence offer alternatives to simultaneous refusal of tribute and family warfare. A partner's promise should be tested against the route or contingent it can actually control. Improving one relationship can free resources for another frontier without requiring the prince to abandon every inherited interest or treat every neighboring claim as an immediate military challenge.

[Costs and contraction] Appanages give relatives a stake in survival but complicate military contributions and courts. Defined assessments and rotating defense can sustain cooperation. After a setback, preserve people, seed, animals, and connected northern towns, using a truce to restore production. Patrimonial prestige supports renewed assembly only when there are residents and usable roads behind it. Defending a claim at the cost of those assets may leave a prince with less authority than a limited settlement whose obligations can still be met and whose communities remain willing to provide assistance.
navarre:
[Two positions and routes across the mountains] Navarre's principal positions are Pamplona and Javier Castle between Pyrenean passages and approaches toward the Ebro. Valleys constrain invading armies but also funnel goods, animals, and supplies through limited routes and crossings. A guarded pass is not permanent security without provisions. Farming, pastoral activity, town markets, and passing merchants provide different resources. Pilgrimage and commerce can generate income while requiring roads, lodging, and protection from repeated charges. Champagne is another royal inheritance whose nobles, towns, and merchants retain separate rights. Interests on either side are not interchangeable, and transfers require passage through other jurisdictions. Connections across regions are an advantage; neighboring control over access is the corresponding vulnerability. A blockade can therefore have consequences out of proportion to the kingdom's small territorial size.

[Dynasty and chartered limits] Theobald II inherited Navarre in 1253, also ruling Champagne and Brie as Theobald V. He belongs to the House of Blois and came to power young, making regency and aristocratic cooperation important to royal government. Confirmation of the fueros imposes constraints on judgment and counsel. Religious recognition strengthens royal standing while local nobles continue to defend their established part in courts and counsel. Close French connections provide support rather than establishing that France has already absorbed the kingdom. Practical legitimacy continues to depend on willingness to meet fiscal and defensive obligations. A general assertion of absolute monarchy would conceal the continuing negotiations through which the crown actually operates, especially during a young ruler's effort to consolidate his position.

[Income exchanged for rights] Royal property, urban markets, passage dues, and local obligations provide plausible resources, while charters and additional payments can form the basis of cooperation with towns. The king wants more reliable administration and income; urban supporters want jurisdictional protection and standing. This exchange does not mean all townspeople benefit equally or that cultivators can bear unlimited demands. Payments and services vary by locality. Effective receipts depend on charters, agents, and transport; without checking local accounts the court may mistake promised money for available coin. Champagne relationships assist commerce and diplomacy without providing costless transfers from a French treasury. Predictable charges for travelers and defined rights for communities may sustain more revenue than one exceptional levy followed by avoidance or refusal.

[Mountain defense and mobilization] Noble followers, local forces, and urban defenders perform different tasks. A summons cannot produce unlimited heavy cavalry. Pamplona supports assembly and provisioning; Javier and other approaches require grain, repair, and rotation. Difficult terrain burdens domestic transport as well as foreign armies. Mounted troops can screen routes and support positions without replacing gate guards, infantry, or road maintenance. Service depends on rights and compensation, while towns may demand clear limits on financial and manpower contributions. A distant expedition removes people who might otherwise defend the homeland or gather the harvest. French assistance requires separate agreement and depends on other wars, musters, and travel time. Expected relief cannot replace local grain stores and dependable watch.

[Kinship diplomacy and frontiers] Theobald's1255 marriage to Isabella, daughter of Louis IX, creates a significant relationship for support and arbitration. Competition between Castile and Aragon can constrain Navarre but also opens possibilities for bargaining instead of immediate warfare. Port access and protected movement can yield more practical value than pressing every territorial claim; recognized rights and physical possession remain distinct. French assistance has its own dynastic interests and cannot guarantee priority for Navarre in every dispute. For the crown, secure approaches around Pamplona and dependable local cooperation are more urgent than a general war beyond a small realm's resources. Every promise of distant service must be weighed against needs on both sides of the mountains, lest the core retain royal titles without adequate defenders.

[Bishops, boroughs, and the court] Pamplona's bishop and the crown compete over jurisdiction, while boroughs and their inhabitants have their own claims. Royal urban alliances can deepen friction with nobles or churchmen. Assigning every inhabitant to an enemy camp by language or origin would obscure disputes over courts, markets, and property. Unresolved disputes over courts and markets can encourage boroughs to place separate defenses above common security, while royal favoritism may widen existing divisions. The young ruler must also manage relationships on both sides of the Pyrenees; prolonged absence can leave local quarrels unresolved. Arbitration, confirmation of rights, continued truces, and limits on extraordinary demands remain usable alternatives if resources fail. Preserving a community able to negotiate and perform obligations may secure the crown more effectively than ceremonial assertions of still greater power.
nicaea:
[Land and sea wings] Nicaea, Smyrna, Bithynia, and western Greek positions lie far apart, with distinct risks on sea and land. Anatolian agriculture supports the regime, while Balkan armies need shipping, stores, and local cooperation. An imperial title does not make every resource available simultaneously. The government must preserve routes from producing districts and decide which garrisons can receive relief. A western opportunity may be valuable but still impose an eastern cost if troops, horses, and money are removed from the frontier that sustains the court.

[Succession and shared power] John III and Theodore II left fiscal and military foundations. John IV's inheritance and Michael's military and political strength create tension within the regime. Roman legitimacy, noble recognition, and ecclesiastical positions constrain the court; achievement does not automatically annul dynastic promises. Securing agreement about office, guardianship, and service can be as consequential as winning a frontier campaign. The ruler needs support that survives a redistribution of rewards, rather than an assumption that every official or commander values imperial recovery above the rights of the house or institution he serves.

[Agriculture and privileges] Land, royal estates, towns, and exchange sustain officials and troops, while privileges and ecclesiastical rights limit collection. Storage, military horses, transport, and pay are present costs. Commercial concessions may purchase naval help while reducing later port receipts. Assessments therefore need to distinguish nominal output, local retention, and resources that can reach the army. Imagined wealth in a contested city cannot pay current wages. Protecting production and setting clear limits on contributions helps the regime mobilize again when an expedition lasts longer than its supporters expected.

[Field forces and maritime tools] Cavalry, infantry, local levies, and outside contingents need different supplies. Siege and straits operations require equipment and ships beyond a field army. Maintain eastern guards and a mobile reserve, seeking a port or route that can be supported before widening objectives. Allied service periods and shares of gains need agreement before commitment. Otherwise a promising concentration can dissolve when partners return home or disagree over a stronghold, leaving the regime with another position to provision and fewer troops available to protect its established districts.

[Latin and regional competitors] The Latin court, Venice, Genoa, Bulgaria, and Rum may cooperate on one matter and compete on another. Religious affinity does not guarantee relief, while commercial privileges need local enforcement. Intelligence, marriage, exchange, and truces can be used separately to reduce simultaneous war. A partner seeking advantage against another maritime power may offer ships for a specific concession without accepting the regime's wider goals. The court should judge the bargain by protection and access it can deliver, rather than by an assertion of permanent allegiance.

[Court costs and fallback] Nobles seek rewards, officials protect revenue, churchmen value sworn obligations, and soldiers require dependable pay. An expedition sustained by confiscation and extraordinary demands can narrow support at home. After a setback, preserve agriculture and a negotiable place for the heir and important commanders, holding connected sea and land positions through local truces. Time gained is useful when it restores money and cooperation. Continuing for prestige alone may consume the very institutions, people, and routes that allow the regime to claim and exercise Roman government.
norway:
[Coastal network] Bergen, Stavanger, Arendal, Oslo, and Lödöse are connected by sea. Fjords provide anchorages while increasing overland distance. Seasons, crews, and stored food determine relief, and northern fish products require exchange with districts supplying grain. The crown needs protected approaches and markets as well as ships. A port's value comes from the people and supplies it can gather, not simply from its position on a long coastline. Keeping a coastal route open may therefore take precedence over an impressive but isolated claim in distant waters.

[Kingship and recognition] Haakon has ruled since 1217. Skule's rebellion ended in 1240, and coronation in 1247 strengthened ecclesiastical recognition. Stability offers opportunities for officers and legal order, but local assemblies, bishops, and nobles continue to bargain over receipts and service. A guarantee that encourages cooperation can be more useful than a unilateral demand that cannot be enforced. The king must preserve support across regions whose immediate concerns differ, giving them reasons to accept common decisions even when an expedition offers most of its rewards elsewhere.

[Resources and exchange] Fish products, cultivation, royal estates, markets, and shipping charges provide resources, while church property and local rights limit collection. An expedition requires equipment and food before gains arrive. The value of a cargo is not royal cash. Dependable merchant relations can bring grain and credit, but privileges may also reduce the income of particular local holders. Agreements need to make those costs visible and identify what protection or supply is obtained, rather than assume every increase in overseas trade automatically strengthens the court by the same amount.

[Ship service and retainers] Household men, noble followings, and local ship service have distinct terms, with equipment and provisions to be divided beforehand. Familiarity with coastal waters does not remove the risks of long voyages. Weather can separate a fleet, and a plan needs protected assembly points and a route home. Port defense and a western expedition require a reserve and replacement crews. Requisitioning all fishing vessels may enlarge a gathering briefly while damaging the households expected to provide food and answer the next summons.

[Islands and neighboring crowns] Scotland takes an interest in western islands, Denmark and Sweden influence southern routes, and island lords retain rights of their own. Marriage, tribute, commerce, and recognition of overlordship can be negotiated separately. One marginal dispute need not become war with every neighboring crown. A distant partner should be assessed by the ships, food, or passage it can actually provide. A formal submission may still require repeated local negotiation, particularly when the obligation competes with fishing, harvests, or the defense of an island's own harbor.

[Local costs and fallback] Legal and fiscal consolidation affects the customs of nobles, churches, and residents. Those asked to serve need enforceable protection and a stated return. After a setback overseas, preserve crews, vessels, core ports, and grain imports, using limited concessions to obtain repair time. Retaining a network that can assemble again is more useful than maintaining an unsupported maritime claim. A settlement that leaves local partners willing to cooperate can protect royal standing better than another expedition financed by exhausting the same coastal communities.
papal:
[Rome and Ancona] The Tiber, roads through Latium, and an Adriatic port connect the principal holdings. Mountains and local barriers prevent revenue and supplies from moving automatically. Holding Rome does not make every surrounding noble or town obedient. Food, envoys, and pilgrims need protected routes, and a harbor needs agreements over ships and customs. Temporal authority must therefore be exercised through specific officers and partners rather than inferred from the pope's broader religious standing across Latin Christendom.

[Pontifical office and temporal authority] Alexander IV was elected in 1254. Petrine succession and canon law support his authority, while cardinals, bishops, religious orders, and towns perform different functions. Religious recognition and military service need separate implementation. The pope's standing among the faithful does not make all of them directly taxable subjects. Even within the temporal territories, inherited rights and communal expectations shape obedience. Appointments, arbitration, and guarantees over property can secure assistance where an assertion of universal jurisdiction would leave practical duties unresolved.

[Income and credit] Estates, ecclesiastical receipts, local dues, and voluntary or negotiated assistance provide money. Exemptions, allocations, and war debts reduce the balance. Collection across realms requires clerical implementation and political cooperation; an appeal does not establish payment already received. Envoys, courts, and guards need continuing support. The government must know which receipts can be used without violating an existing promise. Repeated extraordinary demands may secure one contribution but reduce confidence among the institutions whose help is needed for another mission or defense.

[Allied forces and garrisons] Temporal defense relies on local forces, paid contingents, and allies rather than an army drawn automatically from all Europe. Excommunication can change political costs but cannot replace food, wages, or siege equipment. Partners need duration, compensation, and a defined objective. A campaign becomes dangerous when a religious appeal is interpreted as an unlimited commitment unsupported by transport or money. Keeping reliable guards and communications may preserve more freedom of action than dispersing resources among every claimant who seeks papal endorsement.

[Sicily and the Empire] Manfred, rival imperial candidates, English and French royalty, and Italian cities have interests of their own. Papal recognition is an instrument with costs. Supporting a prince creates questions of debt, service, and local acceptance, so his ability to deliver assistance requires assessment. A title granted abroad may not persuade residents to change allegiance. Mediation and local peace remain useful alongside pressure, allowing the court to separate a dynastic claim from the immediate need to keep roads, markets, and ecclesiastical institutions functioning.

[Local compromise and fallback] Communal autonomy, noble property, and ecclesiastical exemptions constrain collection. Excessive military demands may make supporters regard a religious dispute as a threat to their own resources. Defined contributions, arbitration, and protection can obtain more durable service. After a setback, retain core towns, records, and communications and rebuild alliances through negotiation. Committing all prestige to one Sicilian expedition would leave fewer tools when a partner fails. Authority remains more useful when it can still mediate and protect than when every local disagreement becomes another unaffordable war.
pereyaslavl:
[Dnieper and frontier routes] Pereyaslav, Lubny, Oster, Rylsk, and Putyvl lie across river networks and the steppe edge, combining transport value with military danger. Crossings need boats and shore roads, while wooden defenses need residents and supplies. A marked settlement is not necessarily a prosperous revenue district. The ruler must connect warning and refuge as well as collection. Routes that bring merchants may also bring an army, so provisions for withdrawing people and animals should accompany plans to protect commercial passage.

[Princely standing and external recognition] Patrimony, neighboring relationships, and Mongol authority shape local government, while churches and towns continue to need protection. Arrangements after conquest need not be identical everywhere. Implementation depends on negotiation and people who can enforce it. The presence of an envoy or a particular group does not establish a uniform direct administration across every district. The prince must obtain a usable agreement over assessment, service, and passage while retaining enough local confidence for residents to remain and provide support.

[Limited resources] Estates, cultivation, livestock, fishing and woodland products, and markets can support guards, while tribute and transport take a share of surplus. Restoring land requires seed and labor to remain in place. An extraordinary demand that consumes production leaves neither the next assessment nor the garrison secure. Collection should fit what communities can provide, not a remembered level of prosperity. Protecting a small dependable receipt can be more useful than claiming a large amount whose enforcement encourages flight or strips households of the animals needed to cultivate.

[Crossings and withdrawal] Retainers and local guards can warn, protect stores, and hold restricted approaches. Forces without spare horses should avoid a prolonged pursuit. Castles need agreed messengers, relief arrangements, and evacuation instructions, since defending every isolated point can allow an attacker to surround them in turn. Rotating service protects harvests and winter preparation. The military aim is to retain people, supplies, and a force able to defend again, not merely to keep a flag at a position after its route of relief has disappeared.

[Neighbors and the khan] Kyiv, Chernigov, and other Rus lands may cooperate over exchange or tribute while competing over family rights. Envoys, safe-conducts, and local truces can reduce isolation. Terms of dependence need to fit time and ability to pay. Nominal submission cannot replace protection of an actual road or crossing. Reliable intermediaries help distinguish a promise made at a court from what a local holder will permit, allowing the prince to obtain practical relief without pretending all neighboring disputes have been settled.

[Community costs and fallback] Residents need fields and refuge, nobles seek patrimony, churches protect property, and guards need food. Giving any one an unlimited priority damages the others. After a setback, reduce exposed posts, preserve connected towns and inhabitants, and obtain time through payment extensions and restored exchange. These choices retain the means to fortify and assemble again. Continuing an unsupported defense may instead sacrifice the communities on whose recovery the ruler's longer-term authority and revenue both depend.
pisa:
[River port and islands] Pisa connects to Tuscany through the Arno and its maritime approaches, while Cagliari links Sardinian resources and sailing routes. Harbor security, navigability, warehouses, and inland roads together determine receipts. An island holding does not command every local lord or cargo. The commune needs arrangements about grain, crews, and access to anchorages as well as commercial rights. A distant station can add opportunity while demanding a convoy and a garrison, so its value must be judged against the support required to keep it usable.

[Commune and family rights] Civic offices, councils, and merchant families form the governing network. Ghibelline connections supply diplomatic language without establishing identical interests forever. Sardinian institutions and family succession need particular recognition. Naval prestige alone cannot impose service at every station. Agreements that specify jurisdiction and a share of gains can make cooperation durable, whereas an undefined claim to command may invite a local holder to seek another patron. The commune must therefore distinguish its formal rights from the support officials and merchants can actually obtain.

[Dues and borrowing] Ports, markets, property, and commercial contributions support the commune, while private partnerships and public borrowing need repayment. A warship requires food, oars, sails, and crews before a prize is taken. Interrupted trade can weaken both revenue and access to loans. Excessive collection also reduces willingness to support another naval effort. Predictable charges and protection of contracts may bring a steadier return than a higher levy that makes traders choose a different port or leaves shipowners disputing who must bear the losses.

[Fleet and land defense] Galleys, transports, and civic troops have different uses, and pursuit at sea cannot replace a guarded port. Seasons, repairs, and water limit operations, while paid troops consume money. Before sailing, the commune needs a route back and adequate home defense. Tuscan opponents may exploit a maritime commitment. A limited convoy or attack with clear duration can preserve ships for later service, while a campaign widened for prestige can leave both overseas partners and the home port expecting support the government no longer has.

[Genoa and regional alignments] Genoa, Florence, Lucca, imperial princes, and Levantine stations affect different interests. Islands, convoys, and customs can be negotiated separately, and a land faction need not become permanent war on every sea route. A distant privilege matters only if local authorities can protect it and ships can reach it. Embassies should assess enforcement and costs as well as favorable wording, retaining alternatives when one ally cannot provide the promised access or expects a contribution that would expose Pisa's own defenses.

[Distribution and fallback] Families, shipowners, craftsmen, and taxpayers bear losses differently. Rewards and compensation need to be deliverable. If land and sea pressures coincide, preserve the home port, food shipments, and credit, reducing isolated commitments and seeking a truce. Maintaining a society able to build ships and mobilize again provides more lasting security than a claim to dominate every sea. A bargain that retains markets and willing contributors may strengthen the commune more than an additional victory whose costs remain unpaid and disputed at home.
poland:
[Rivers and regions] Kraków, Sandomierz, Poznań, Wrocław, Płock, and Gdańsk connect the Vistula, Oder, and routes to the sea. Each region has its own castles and markets. Southern salt and northern shipping need transport and local agreements before they yield resources available elsewhere. A crossing can join regions, but the holder of its castle and toll rights determines practical access.

[Seniority and branches] Bolesław V has held the Kraków position since 1243, while Piast branches continue to contest patrimony and precedence. Churchmen, nobles, and towns give recognition practical force. Seniority must provide justice and protection; descent alone does not oblige every duke to furnish troops for every objective. Confirmations of rights can win support while limiting later demands.

[Salt, estates, and privileges] Salt, estates, markets, minting, and passage rights provide different receipts. Urban and ecclesiastical privileges restrain arbitrary assessment. Settlers, craftsmen, and exchange can rebuild dependable revenue, while war loans need a means of repayment. Repeated demands on the same villages damage both the next harvest and willingness to support common defense.

[Castles and mobilization] Ducal retainers, noble cavalry, town guards, and local levies serve on different terms. The invasion of 1241 gives reason to value crossings, scouting, and avoiding encirclement. Regional assistance needs agreements on food, command, and return. An assembled host is not a standing army, and leaving every castle to join one battle may expose the communities that provision it.

[Neighbors and diplomacy] Hungarian marriages, Rus kinship, northern orders, and western princes provide different channels. Passage and jurisdiction can be negotiated before land disputes are resolved. Church mediation and nonaggression reduce simultaneous threats, but an ally's oath needs deliverable troops or provisions. Support for one claim should not silently become an obligation to finance every quarrel of its holder.

[Domestic costs and fallback] Branches fear losing patrimony, towns fear exactions, and churches defend exemptions. Forced unity can combine these concerns into opposition. Limited service, rotating defense, and explicit contributions preserve cooperation. After a setback, hold connected castles and protect seed and residents, rebuilding common defense through marriage and recognition rather than an unaffordable campaign against every dissenting relative.
polotsk:
[Dvina and connecting routes] The Western Dvina leads toward the Baltic, while Vitebsk, Minsk, Zaslauje, and Braslau connect inland districts. Water levels, seasons, portage, and rights along the banks limit traffic. Commercial value depends on willing merchants and protection. Control of a river town does not automatically secure the whole route or allow its ruler to collect the value of every cargo.

[Princely and local rights] Rus princely tradition, towns, and churches sustain recognition, while Lithuanian power also influences local relationships. Dependence and jurisdiction need implementation in each district. Patrimony is not an unlimited command right. Confirmation of succession and local institutions can obtain cooperation, but the ruler must specify what service and protection accompany that recognition.

[Markets and receipts] Estates, markets, passage, and exchange yield resources shared with local holders and ecclesiastical institutions. Consistent agreements and settlement of debts and disputes support repeated collection. Seizing cargo may bring an immediate gain while damaging credit and raising escort costs. The ruler needs to protect the producers and traders whose activity makes a toll worth holding.

[Defense and river transport] Princely forces and town guards protect landing places, crossings, and roads. Boats carry food subject to water conditions. Forests and wetlands delay attackers and relief alike. Warning and assistance need prior agreement. Sending every available fighter away can expose the very trading node whose receipts are expected to finance the expedition.

[Lithuania and the Baltic approaches] Lithuanian lords, Riga, Livonian powers, and other Rus lands have separate commercial, tributary, and territorial interests. Religious difference does not exclude trade, and an alliance need not include every foreign war. Envoys should specify safety, charges, and compensation. Agreements are valuable when the authority granting them can protect the route in question.

[Autonomy and fallback] Nobles seek patrimony, towns seek exchange, and churches defend rights. External protection brings service demands. Defined contributions and jurisdictional limits sustain cooperation. In crisis, preserve people and Dvina communications through limited concessions, then renegotiate from a functioning base rather than leave the city isolated in a siege without dependable relief.
portugal:
[Atlantic towns and river valleys] The principal Portuguese positions are Porto, Coimbra, Lisbon, Branco Castle, and Beja Castle, connecting the Douro, Mondego, Tagus, and southern interior. River mouths assist exchange without making every upstream reach navigable by loaded vessels. Transshipment, shallows, seasonal conditions, and road links still impose costs. Agriculture, wine, salt, fish, livestock, and local manufacture sustain towns; coastal livelihoods depend first on familiar waters and dependable exchange. Conquest in the Algarve adds resources and defense obligations. Settlement, garrisons, and inhabitants' rights require continuing arrangements; lands named in a title do not all deliver freely disposable surpluses. Lisbon provides a commercial and royal base while older northern centers retain noble, ecclesiastical, and local interests. Resources do not automatically flow toward one unquestioned capital.

[The crown after displacement] Afonso III is the son of Afonso II and brother of Sancho II, with previous ties to Boulogne through marriage and title. Following papal intervention in 1245 he entered Portugal under a claim to protect and govern the kingdom. Sancho's death in 1248 ended the presence of another living king. Afonso's authority therefore draws on dynasty, ecclesiastical recognition, and supporters rather than an entirely uncontested succession. The1249 Algarve conquest strengthens his title and prestige without settling every Castilian claim. His1253 marriage to Alfonso X's daughter Beatrice supplies a diplomatic connection but also raises questions involving his prior marriage. The crown still needs ecclesiastical recognition and cannot settle marriage or jurisdiction simply through unilateral commands.

[Charters, inquiry, and income] Estate revenues, market and harbor charges, local obligations, and extraordinary grants support government, while charters offer towns more predictable terms. The Leiria Cortes of 1254 included municipal representatives, giving the crown a means to seek urban cooperation while towns continued to defend their particular rights. Urban support must still be renewed through particular negotiations and credible protection. Inquiry into rights and land held by nobles or churches may recover resources claimed by the crown but provokes resistance from holders. Unpredictable changes in money, dues, and requisitions can undermine commercial cooperation. Muslim inhabitants and other communities also possess livelihoods and property interests after conquest. Newly acquired land is not an empty resource awaiting unrestricted extraction.

[Service and southern defense] Household followers, noble retinues, municipal forces, and military orders have different duties. Cavalry can patrol, raid, and pursue while garrisons require infantry, grain, and repairs. These organizations cannot all become a permanently available professional army. New southern possessions need roads, markets, and settled inhabitants as well as celebration of victory. Excessive levies remove labor and interrupt production. Shipping can assist transport and coastal watch, but requisition takes vessels and crews away from normal earnings. Coastal watch requires experienced pilots as well as arrangements for harbors, fresh water, and rotation. Existing maritime capacity grows from fisheries, nearby trade, and practical seafaring, constrained by weather, provisions, and the availability of financing. A port alone does not establish permanent command of distant waters.

[The Algarve question and neighboring powers] Castile advances claims concerning the southern conquest while Portugal reinforces actual possession through local grants and government. Marriage, truces, and exchanges of rights offer possible accommodations. Boundaries, titles, and recognized rights remain matters for negotiation; marriage does not settle every disagreement. Aragonese and Italian merchants can be partners as well as competitors, and protecting Atlantic commerce does not require participation in every Mediterranean conflict. The contraction of Muslim political power does not remove local disputes over property or security. The immediate diplomatic interest is to prevent a war over competing titles from consuming possessions already held, while maintaining exchange between inland districts and Atlantic ports. Neither side's claims should be confused with the forces it can actually deploy.

[Churches, magnates, and municipalities] Interests that assisted Afonso's rise do not cease to defend themselves afterward. Churches claim property and jurisdictional exemptions, magnates maintain local influence, and towns welcome royal protection while contesting additional demands. Municipal representation does not make towns unanimous or fully represent every poor household and cultivator. Simultaneous pressure on ecclesiastical holdings, noble possessions, and commerce could erode cooperation. Ecclesiastical recognition affects marriage, jurisdiction, and the public standing of kingship; religious conflict cannot be treated merely as another property lawsuit. Inquiry supported by evidence, clear adjudication, and predictable collection provide alternatives to unchecked confrontation. When southern claims cannot be resolved immediately, restrained commitments and continued negotiation preserve more useful resources than staking every source of credit on rights the crown cannot yet defend.
rum:
[Plateau routes] Konya, Ankara, Kayseri, and western castles are linked by plateau roads. Caravan facilities, water, and winter grain determine movement. Agriculture and urban exchange sustain forces, while mountain routes and seasons raise transport costs. Possession of one city cannot guarantee safety at the far end of a commercial road; local officials and neighboring holders must cooperate.

[Dynasty and supervision] Defeat at Köse Dağ in 1243 made Mongol authority a central condition of dynastic policy. Kaykaus, Kilij Arslan, and their supporters compete within arrangements of shared power. A sultanic title still requires obedience from officials, revenue districts, and armed followers. Recognition from a superior court may strengthen a claim without settling all rival jurisdictions at home.

[Assessment and commerce] Agriculture, markets, property, and passage support the court and caravan facilities, while tribute, service, and local retention reduce the balance. Protected roads and enforceable charges encourage trade. Repeated extraordinary demands harm villages, craftsmen, and merchants, reducing later collection and credit. Fiscal officers need clear responsibility so rival patrons do not demand the same surplus twice.

[Court and frontier forces] Royal troops, local lords, Turkish mounted followers, and castle guards have distinct obligations. Mobile forces need horses and pasture, while sieges need craftsmen and stores. Mongol service can remove home defenders, so duration and replacement require agreement. A field victory that leaves roads and producing districts unguarded may weaken the regime's ability to sustain another campaign.

[Neighbors and diplomacy] Nicaea, Armenia, Mongol commanders, and Anatolian local powers seek different security and revenue interests. Exile, marriage, and dependence offer bargaining tools but can provoke suspicion. Truces, passage, and local recognition should be pursued separately. A partner may grant refuge or access without accepting an obligation to restore every claim of the person it protects.

[Distribution and fallback] Succession struggles and repeated collection encourage local holders to seek another protector. Restraint of private exactions and affordable obligations can retain support. If eastern pressure increases, preserve food routes, fiscal personnel, and core defenders through limited concessions.
