Restored production and credible administration provide a basis for adjusting the frontier; a nominally larger realm stripped of both cannot support recovery.
rus:
[Rivers, lakes, and grain] The Volkhov, Lake Ilmen, and routes toward the Baltic and upper Volga sustain Novgorod. Torzhok, Pskov, and Velikiye Luki guard different approaches. Northern goods do not replace imported grain. Interruptions to shipping or markets can quickly affect the city, so warehouses, crossings, and agreements with producing districts matter alongside the wealth of distant tributary territories.

[Civic authority and the prince] Assemblies, the posadnik, archbishop, and boyar networks share influence. A prince provides military service under conditions. Groups disagree over appointments, tribute, and courts. Defending civic autonomy requires enforceable terms rather than the absence of lordship or hierarchy. Recognition of a prince is useful when it brings protection without leaving duties and local jurisdiction undefined.

[Exchange and tribute resources] Furs, wax, property, markets, and transit yield resources, but distant collection needs intermediaries, labor, and transport. Merchant profit is not public revenue, and ecclesiastical and boyar rights disperse receipts. Dependable debt judgments and commercial agreements protect credit more effectively than arbitrary seizure. A nominal tribute district may cost more to maintain than its immediate delivery suggests.

[Forces and frontiers] Princely followers, civic troops, and local contingents perform different defensive tasks. Western strongpoints and lake-and-river routes need guards. Experience in 1240 and 1242 supports warning and terrain judgment without guaranteeing another victory. Expeditions and service in northern districts also affect food and exchange, making duration and replacement important parts of any military agreement.

[Western powers and the khan] Sweden, Livonian powers, German merchants, and the khan affect frontiers, commerce, and assessment in different ways. They are not a single enemy. Passage, compensation, and tribute can be negotiated while preserving religious and judicial interests. Separating these matters reduces the risk of losing both a military protector and the partners who keep grain arriving.

[Social costs and fallback] Boyars, ordinary residents, and collectors bear and receive different shares. Forced assessments can intensify civic disputes. Defined sums, installments, and rotating defense preserve cooperation. If the frontier worsens, keep granaries, markets, and western passage open through a limited truce or compensation. Exhausting the city to defend a peripheral claim would weaken the base from which local rights can be defended again.
scotland:
[Geography] Lowland cultivation and east-coast ports provide food and exchange, while Highland roads, western coasts, and islands need guides and ships. The southern frontier and western waters have different supply requirements. Seasons and distance constrain assembly and relief.

[Legitimacy] Alexander III succeeded as a child in 1249. Noble guardianship and marriage connections with England influence the court. Inheritance does not extinguish local rights; appointments, justice, and service require practical recognition from those expected to implement royal decisions.

[Revenue] Estates, markets, ports, and local obligations support the crown alongside church and noble rights. Voyages require advance supplies. Nominal island tribute is not money already received. Dependable justice and exchange protect receipts that can support another mobilization.

[Forces] Household troops, noble followings, and local levies serve on different terms. Cavalry, infantry, and ships suit different tasks. Border defense, ports, and western operations need separate allocations; harvests and crews' livelihoods limit a prolonged gathering.

[Diplomacy] England, Norway, island lords, and domestic magnates pursue different interests. Marriage does not imply obedience in every foreign matter, and island recognition needs deliverable service. Commerce, arbitration, and local truces can reduce simultaneous conflict.

[Costs and fallback] Favoring one court faction can drive others toward foreign patrons, while excessive service harms production. Define jurisdictions and burdens. After a setback, preserve Lowland food, ports, and royal credit, rebuilding support through negotiation before renewing distant claims.
serbia:
[Geography] Inland valleys lead toward Kosovo and the Adriatic. Mines and ports require pack transport, passes, and protection between them. Mountains aid defense but slow collection and relief; towns cannot assist one another merely according to their straight-line distance.

[Legitimacy] Uroš I has ruled since 1243, supported by Nemanjić descent and the autonomous church. Royal relatives, churches, and nobles retain property and jurisdictions. Appointments and service must be arranged as an acceptable exchange rather than assumed from dynastic standing alone.

[Revenue] Mining at Brskovo, estates, and markets provide receipts. Privileges encourage skilled workers and traders while limiting exactions. Silver must be extracted, processed, and transported before it funds troops. Military demands must leave timber, labor, and food available for continued production.

[Forces] Retainers, noble cavalry, and local guards operate around passes and fortresses. Expeditions require fodder, food, and defined service. Silver can hire troops without instantly replacing training or horses. Both inland approaches and coastal connections need defenders left behind.

[Diplomacy] Hungary, Bulgaria, Nicaea, and coastal towns affect different borders and routes. Religious affinity does not eliminate disputes. Passage, marriage, and charges can be negotiated separately, keeping a limited alliance from becoming an obligation to fight every opponent of its partner.

[Costs and fallback] Mining and merchant privileges can reduce established lordly gains, while military finance burdens cultivators. Defined shares, church mediation, and local guarantees sustain cooperation. After a setback, hold mines, food routes, and connected mountain fortresses, using a truce to restore cash and manpower.
sicily:
[Two shores and supplies] Sicily and southern Italy connect through Messina. Palermo, Naples, and Taranto serve different routes. Island grain, crews, and ports require dependable exchange. If the strait is interrupted, political unity cannot readily become military strength across both shores.

[Crown and recognition] Manfred was crowned in 1258 amid conflicting Hohenstaufen claims and papal opposition. Recognition by lords and towns shapes practical government. Royal institutions provide continuity without eliminating competing views of succession or the rights attached to it.

[Revenue] Agriculture, estates, ports, and royal administration provide receipts limited by church and local rights. Collection must preserve production and credit. Commercial profit is not wholly royal income. Ships, war, and paid troops need continuing cash that confiscation cannot reliably replace.

[Forces] Noble cavalry, royal troops, Muslim contingents, and ships perform different tasks. Island defense, the strait, and northern campaigning compete for pay, food, and crews. Allied service needs defined duration; a land victory cannot substitute for secure transport between the shores.

[Neighbors] The papacy, Lombard powers, maritime republics, and Mediterranean crowns can enable or obstruct help. Ghibelline association does not guarantee unlimited assistance. Marriage and passage need specific returns, while commercial cooperation can continue despite a dispute about the crown.

[Costs and fallback] Groups expect different terms of taxation, courts, and service. Protection of rights and shared defense reduce defection. After a setback, preserve island grain, the strait, and reliable guards through a limited truce, preventing imperial prestige from exhausting the resources of the kingdom actually held.
smolensk:
[Communications] The upper Dnieper and Western Dvina require overland transfer, limited by water levels, seasons, and labor. The town network must protect crossings and roads. Position on a major route does not make the full value of its cargo available to the prince.

[Patrimony and towns] Rostislavichi tradition and churches support princely standing alongside urban and family interests in courts, property, and succession. Confirmation of holdings and acceptable officials builds recognition. A distant dynastic claim does not deliver local receipts.

[Resources] Estates, markets, transfer, and exchange provide receipts constrained by commercial agreements and local rights. Credible judgments and escorts encourage repeated trade. Arbitrary seizure undermines lending and confidence. Roads, guards, and external obligations all draw on the balance.

[Defense] Retainers, towns, and local forces can hold crossings and forest routes but cannot campaign abroad while guarding every approach. Warning, stores, and rotating service need agreement. Walls cannot restore food if an attacker bypasses the city to damage its producing districts.

[Neighbors] Polotsk, Lithuania, Chernigov, northeastern Rus, and Riga merchants pursue distinct interests. Commerce can continue before territorial disputes are settled. Family guarantees and limited truces reduce isolation; religious affinity does not establish military aid already available.

[Costs and fallback] Princely expansion affects noble and urban shares, while privileges reduce older charges. Define service and distributions. After a setback, preserve residents, crossings, and stores through limited concessions rather than exhaust trade, then reopen claims from a base with restored credit.
swedish:
[Routes and regions] Mälaren, the Baltic, and southern ports connect different districts, with separate hinterlands around Linköping, Skara, and Växjö. Visby's commercial value depends on crews and agreements. Waterways do not replace local roads and stores or make every region's resources available to the court at once.

[Authority] Valdemar was elected in 1250, while Birger's family, military standing, and appointments provide practical support. Nobles and churches influence recognition. Legal consolidation needs acceptable officials and implementation, rather than an assumption that descent alone commands each district.

[Revenue] Agriculture, estates, markets, passage, and port dues yield different receipts limited by privileges and local rights. Protecting exchange enlarges dependable income, while ship service and expeditions consume labor, timber, and food otherwise needed for production.

[Forces] Noble cavalry, regional levies, and ships suit different tasks. Eastern garrisons need supply and replacements. Forests, ice, sailing seasons, and castles shape operations. Service cannot remain detached from cultivation indefinitely, and expeditions require a reserve at home.

[Diplomacy] Novgorod, Denmark, Norway, merchants, and Finnish local holders affect different borders and exchange. Religion and family ties open negotiations without guaranteeing obedience. Passage, limited payments, and recognition can be pursued before a general war.

[Costs and fallback] Stronger justice may reduce noble gains, while port privileges alter distributions. Defined duties preserve cooperation. After a setback, reduce eastern commitments and protect food routes and core ports, using a truce to restore crews and credit before another expansion.
teutonic:
[Regions and communications] Prussian and Livonian positions are separated by distance, with different needs at river mouths, coasts, and forest roads. Riga, Elbing, Königsberg, and inland forts provide anchors without making all intervening land secure. Stores and protected movement determine whether they can assist one another.

[Order and jurisdiction] The grand master, regional officers, bishops, and towns have distinct duties and rights. The rule provides order without eliminating competition. Papal and princely recognition supports action, but possession, assessment, and local obedience still require implementation.

[Resources] Donations, estates, markets, and local contributions sustain forces. Settlement and cultivation need time and protection. Privileges attract people while limiting exactions. A new fort is not immediately a net gain: repairs, transport, and guards create continuing expenses.

[Military] Brothers, paid troops, local forces, and visiting crusaders have different tasks and service periods. Castles need water and food and cannot be emptied for an expedition. Forests, wetlands, and mobile opponents require reconnaissance and withdrawal plans; masonry does not replace trained guards.

[Neighbors] Lithuanian and Samogitian leaders, Polish dukes, Rus powers, and coastal merchants pursue different objectives. Baptism or a land grant does not ensure local compliance. Allies need deliverable troops and supplies, while truces and trading routes can be negotiated separately.

[Costs and fallback] Forced service and religious pressure can provoke resistance; land distribution creates disputes among holders. Defined duties and protection reduce isolation. After a setback, preserve river mouths, residents, and connected forts through limited concessions, restoring production rather than make prestige a duty to hold every exposed post.
tlemcen_algeria:
[Ports, fortresses, and dynastic connections] Zayyanid government directly relies on Oran and Melilla Castle, while connections with Tlemcen provide standing and recognition. Claims and disposable resources are different: officials, defenders, and payments must be secured before prestige can provide grain from distant stores. Oran provides Mediterranean exchange and transport while Melilla is a more distant coastal position. Relief must follow actual routes and distances. This region connects movement across the Maghreb with north–south traffic, supported by cultivation, pastoral activity, and urban exchange. A strategically useful route is not an unavoidable monopoly: caravans respond to water, security, and charges, while shipping faces weather, harbor conditions, and predation. Communication between holdings remains a task rather than a geographical guarantee.

[The making of Zayyanid authority] Yaghmurasen emerged from a Zanata background as Almohad control disintegrated. An independent dynastic base emerged around 1235–1236 through local recognition and resistance to the former center, not merely a change in title. The death of the Almohad caliph in the1248 Oujda fighting demonstrates effective resistance to the former superior, not permanent obedience from every tribe thereafter. Followings, urban protection, and religious patronage all matter. Personal followings, urban recognition, and religious standing reinforce one another while entailing different obligations. Military standing helps attract support, but chiefs and towns still judge protection, rewards, and exactions; victory cannot replace regular justice or secure exchange. Recognition must continue to be maintained through action and distribution.

[Traffic, revenue, and pastoral constraints] Tlemcen connects Oran, Morocco, Ifriqiya, and routes toward the Sahara. Goods pass through several authorities providing protection and collecting dues, rather than a gold pipeline owned by one dynasty. Markets, cultivation, and herds produce different resources, while the claims of local leaders affect central access. Central access depends on remittances, safe transport, and granted rights; the entire value of passing goods is not royal income. Distant nodes such as Sijilmasa remain beyond direct command. Desert exchange requires cooperation with chiefs, oasis communities, and guides; a changed water point or additional charge can redirect caravans. Military demands compete with seed, fodder, and the reproduction of herds. Merchants need dependable passage and dispute settlement more than declarations that the desert is controlled. Repeated payments that redirect traffic weaken both income and defense.

[Mounted followings and defended towns] Zanata supporters and other local partners provide mobilization. Cavalry assists patrol, reconnaissance, and raiding without replacing siege equipment, infantry, or transport. Towns need grain and repairs; separated coastal positions need communications, potentially including vessels. Expected booty cannot fund every requirement in advance. Chiefs bringing men and horses possess bargaining power rather than supplying a costless pool owned by the center. Mobilization depends on chiefs' contributions and local pastures. Service time, distance, and rewards require agreement, while replacing lost warhorses takes considerable time and expense. Sending the principal forces away for an extended campaign may expose markets and cultivation around Oran. Defensive success therefore depends on continued production and movement, not solely a reputation for bravery in one encounter.

[Choices between powerful neighbors] Marinid growth to the west and Hafsid authority to the east coexist with surviving Almohad positions, creating several possible alignments rather than a requirement for perpetual war with all. Common religion does not establish a common ruler, and contact with Granada or Castile is not automatically abandonment of belief. Relationships change with frontier pressures and interests; former cooperation does not guarantee relief in every campaign. Presently, avoiding encirclement, retaining port access, and defining protection and frontier terms offer practical objectives. Defense must rely on existing walls, stores, and allies able to arrive. Waiting for an unfulfilled building project or agreement can expose inhabitants to blockade and shortages. Diplomacy can reduce the number of simultaneous military commitments.

[Distribution and a defensible independence] Chiefs seek offices and returns, towns seek stable markets, cultivators and herders need relief from disruption, and religious authorities protect institutions. These are specific claims, not one unanimous national will. Rewards can secure immediate service while dispersing too much future revenue; attempts to reclaim them may alienate previous allies. Under heavy western pressure, localized agreements, recognition of rights, and supportable positions may preserve more independence than a distant expedition beyond available supplies. Yaghmurasen must convince relatives, chiefs, and towns that a shorter front preserves common interests rather than abandoning allies to bear the losses. Protected markets, open food routes, and credible rewards retain a basis for renewed bargaining and future frontier gains.
turov:
[Wetlands and routes] Pripyat channels, marshes, and seasonal water levels shape town connections. Boats, causeways, and local guides determine usable routes. Winter and dry periods alter protection, while isolation also raises the cost of relief and transport.

[Patrimony and recognition] Rus patrimony, appanages, and church recognition support princes, while Pinsk and Turov retain local interests. Family rights need enforceable boundaries and service arrangements. An older common title does not make every relative provide troops unconditionally.

[Livelihood and receipts] Cultivation, fishing, livestock, woodland resources, and exchange sustain communities. Transport losses and local retention reduce the collectable share. Preserving seed, boats, and residents restores enduring income more effectively than repeated demands beyond capacity.

[Defense] Retainers and local forces guard causeways, crossings, and wooden forts. Warning and stores suit the terrain better than extended pursuit. Long service by boatmen interrupts transport. Guards need rotation, and isolated positions need evacuation instructions rather than indefinite reliance on relief.

[Neighbors] Galicia, Lithuania, and other Rus princes have distinct interests in kinship, tribute, and passage. Safe-conducts, marriage, and local truces reduce pressure. External recognition needs actual protection, and avoiding war still requires resources and concessions in negotiation.

[Costs and fallback] Princes, churches, boatmen, and villages bear collection differently. Excessive assembly damages livelihoods. Define tribute and service, then preserve core river towns, seed, and people after a setback, using a truce to restore transport. Governable communities matter more than an empty remote claim.
tver:
[Upper Volga] Tver lies among river junctions and roads toward Novgorod. Passage value depends on crossings, roads, and stores. Food, timber, and urban exchange support residents, while ice and water levels alter movement and supply.

[Prince and family] Yaroslav's relationships provide patrimony and recognition while creating competition among brothers and branches. Churches and towns need protection and justice. Senior claims require force and revenue, not precedence alone.

[Revenue] Estates, markets, crossings, and transit provide limited resources shared among tribute, repairs, and service. Settlement and dependable charges can enlarge receipts. Seizures and repeated exactions damage commerce and the next loan.

[Forces] Retainers, local troops, and guards protect rivers and roads. Timber-and-earth defenses need water and food. Expeditions remove workers and horses, requiring service limits, replacement guards, and warning rather than an unprotected homeland.

[Neighbors] Vladimir, Novgorod, Smolensk, and the khan affect recognition, food, and passage differently. Markets and truces can be negotiated while claims remain unresolved. Investiture does not deliver another land's revenue, and merchants need not become hostages to every political dispute.

[Costs and fallback] Relatives seek land, towns need roads, and nobles expect rewards. Rapid expansion can exhaust support. Define service and jurisdiction. After a setback, preserve river towns, residents, and seed through bounded recognition, rebuilding local strength rather than hold an unsupported senior title.
venice:
[Routes] The lagoon offers shelter and defense, while Zadar, Pula, Ragusa, and Aegean positions serve different routes. Ships, water, stores, and seasons determine relief. The city needs imported food; overseas profit cannot replace a cargo safely arriving at home.

[Institutions] Reniero Zeno, councils, and merchant families influence policy. The doge cannot dispose freely of private shipping. Overseas officers and communities implement privileges and courts. Communal authority needs defined protection and service rather than a claim that all assets belong to the government.

[Revenue] Customs, agreed contributions, and borrowing support fleets, while profits and losses belong to different partnerships. Repairs, convoys, and guards create continuing costs. Repeated demands weaken credit; repayment and contract enforcement support another round of finance.

[Forces] Galleys, transports, garrisons, and temporary levies perform different tasks. Voyages need replacement crews and supplies. Pursuit may expose food routes. Define service and prizes before sailing rather than turn one victory into unlimited convoy obligations.

[Competition] Saint Sabas and the naval fighting at Acre in 1258 shape Genoese relations, while the Latin court, Nicaea, and Pisa seek particular returns. Privileges, naval help, and jurisdiction require separate bargains. Shared religion does not guarantee continuing cooperation.

[Costs and fallback] Merchants need markets, crews need pay, and colonies need protection. War can divide these interests. Preserve contracts and explicit contributions. After a setback, hold the lagoon, food routes, and dependable ports, using a limited truce to rebuild money and ships rather than sacrifice the commune to prestige.
verona:
[Geography] The Adige and southern Alpine roads connect German lands with Lombardy. Verona's castle anchors crossings and approaches. Traffic needs travelers, stores, and security. Holding one gateway does not force every caravan to use it or make every cargo public revenue.

[Authority] Mastino's influence operates through family, civic offices, and supporters. Guilds and established nobles retain rights. Stability depends on courts and appointments negotiated with them; lordly standing does not erase communal politics.

[Revenue] Markets, property, transit, and civic dues supply money distinct from private profit. Guards and wages need a repayable source. Confiscation may fill a gap briefly while driving property holders toward foreign patrons and weakening the next loan.

[Forces] Civic troops, cavalry, and paid forces protect rivers and roads. Expeditions require service periods, supplies, and replacement guards. Mountain approaches and plains require different tactics; a siege elsewhere must not leave the core undefended.

[Neighbors] Mantua, Padua, Lombard powers, and imperial princes have distinct interests. Ghibelline association does not establish unified command. Trade and local peace can precede settlement of land disputes; allied service needs defined limits and a deliverable contribution.

[Costs and fallback] Suppressing opponents can rally supporters while enlarging an exile coalition. Guilds need security rather than unlimited demands. Confirm property and jurisdiction and protect food access. After a setback, retain the city through a truce and rebuild support through credit and office.
vladimir:
[River network] The Klyazma, Oka, and Volga connect northeastern towns. Distance, ice, and crossings constrain collection and relief. Rostov and Suzdal have their own hinterlands, while distant forts need separate support. The realm is not one freely accessible storehouse.

[Seniority and recognition] Alexander combines family, military, and khanate connections. Investiture strengthens authority without removing rivalry. Churches, towns, and lords require protection and justice; princely standing needs concrete arrangements for service and receipts.

[Revenue] Estates, markets, crossings, and assessments sustain government, limited by local retention, church rights, and transport. Preserving residents and seed supports repeated payment. Collection beyond capacity damages later revenue and the legitimacy of those enforcing it.

[Forces] Retainers, local mounted forces, and town guards perform different tasks. Crossings and expeditions compete for horses and food. Warning, replacement guards, and winter stores need agreement; past success cannot guarantee endurance without supply.

[Neighbors] Novgorod, Tver, Ryazan, relatives, and the khan affect exchange, investiture, and borders differently. Tribute, civic courts, and family holdings can be negotiated separately, preventing one disagreement from turning every relationship into a war.

[Costs and fallback] Collectors and payers have different interests, and support needs visible protection. Define assessments and rotating defense. After a setback, preserve people, rivers, and core towns through a limited truce or recognition. Seniority has lasting value when it sustains cooperation.
wales:
[Mountains and coast] Snowdonia, Conwy, and southern coasts have different supply routes. Harlech, Pembroke, Cardiff, and Swansea need guards. Mountains delay enemies and complicate local transport; ports and Lowland production remain essential to sustained defense.

[Princely recognition] Llywelyn strengthened his position during the 1250s and gained princely support for his Welsh title in 1258. Local succession, law, and noble interests remain important. Seniority does not establish direct administration over every holding.

[Revenue] Produce, livestock, markets, and agreed tribute support princes, while war damages pasture and harvests. Repairs, retainers, and ransoms need money and goods. Spoils are not a dependable annual revenue with which to promise permanent service.

[Forces] Local troops, mounted followers, and archers work with narrow approaches and mountain routes. Castles still need food, water, and replacement guards. Raiding and prolonged sieges have different demands. Terrain cannot replace training, command, or the protection of producing districts.

[England and neighboring lords] The English king, marcher lords, and Welsh families do not always follow one policy. Another party may disrupt a local truce. Passage, recognition, and compensation need separate guarantees, keeping an agreement enforceable rather than rejecting every compromise over a title.

[Costs and fallback] Common resistance still requires division of land, spoils, and burdens. Exactions can send local holders to another protector. Confirm rights and protect seed and rotating defense. After a setback, retain core valleys and ports through a truce, rebuilding people and credit for renewed cooperation.
